title: 1  Neural Networks and Optimization
text:
1.1 Overview
This chapter establishes the mathematical and architectural foundations of modern deep learning. Understanding these fundamentals is essential for research scientist interviews, as they underpin all contemporary models—from vision transformers to large language models. We cover the core building blocks (layers, activations, normalization), the learning algorithms (backpropagation, optimization), and the principles that enable generalization.
Key Interview Topics: Network architecture design, gradient flow and vanishing gradients, optimization algorithm selection, regularization strategies, batch normalization mechanics.

title: 1  Neural Networks and Optimization
text:
1.2 Supervised Learning Framework
In supervised learning, we are given a dataset \(\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_1, y_1), \ldots, (\mathbf{x}_m, y_m)\}\), where: - \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\) are input feature vectors - \(y_i \in \mathcal{Y}\) are corresponding targets (labels)
Each pair \((\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\) is assumed to be sampled i.i.d. from some unknown joint distribution \(p(\mathbf{x}, y)\), where \(\mathbf{x} \sim p(\mathbf{x})\) and \(y \sim p(y|\mathbf{x})\).
Learning Objective: Find a function \(f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}\) that approximates the conditional distribution \(p(y|\mathbf{x})\), or equivalently, minimizes the expected prediction error.
Neural networks represent \(f_\theta\) as a composition of simple linear and nonlinear transformations, whose parameters \(\theta\) are optimized to minimize the discrepancy between predictions \(\hat{y}_i = f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i)\) and observed targets \(y_i\).
Why This Matters: Understanding the probabilistic view of supervised learning explains why we use cross-entropy for classification (log-likelihood) and MSE for regression (Gaussian likelihood assumption). In interviews, you may be asked to justify loss function choices or discuss when supervised learning assumptions break down.

title: 1  Neural Networks and Optimization
text:
1.3 Neural Network Architecture

1.3.1 Linear Layers
Definition: A linear (or fully-connected/dense) layer performs an affine transformation:
\[\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}\]
where: - \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\) is the input - \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}}}\) is the weight matrix
- \(\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}\) is the bias vector - \(\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}\) is the pre-activation output
Parameter Count: \(d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}} + d_{\text{out}}\)
Initialization Strategy:

Weights \(\mathbf{W}\): Sample from \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) where \(\sigma\) depends on the initialization scheme:

Xavier/Glorot: \(\sigma^2 = \frac{2}{d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}}\) (for sigmoid/tanh)
He/Kaiming: \(\sigma^2 = \frac{2}{d_{\text{in}}}\) (for ReLU)

Bias \(\mathbf{b}\): Initialize to zero vector

Why Random Initialization? Without randomness, all neurons in a layer would compute identical gradients during backpropagation and remain symmetric. Proper initialization also prevents vanishing/exploding activations in deep networks by keeping variance stable across layers.
Interview Insight: Be prepared to explain why He initialization uses \(2/d_{\text{in}}\) instead of Xavier’s \(2/(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\). The answer relates to ReLU killing half the activations (setting negatives to zero), which requires compensating with larger variance.



1.3.2 Activation Functions
Activation functions introduce non-linearity, enabling networks to learn complex decision boundaries. Without them, stacking linear layers would remain equivalent to a single linear transformation.
Common Activation Functions:

where \(\Phi(z)\) is the cumulative distribution function of standard normal distribution.
Properties and Trade-offs:

Sigmoid/Tanh:

Saturate for large \(|z|\) → gradients vanish → slow learning in deep networks
Still used in gates (LSTMs, GRUs) where squashing to \((0,1)\) is desirable

ReLU:

Computationally efficient (simple thresholding)
Sparse activation (many zeros)
Dying ReLU problem: Neurons with large negative bias may never activate

Leaky ReLU:

Prevents dying ReLU by allowing small negative gradient
Hyperparameter \(\alpha = 0.01\) often works well

GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit):

Smooth approximation to ReLU
Used in Transformers (BERT, GPT)
Allows small negative values to pass through


Interview Question: “Why do modern architectures prefer ReLU over sigmoid?” Answer: ReLU doesn’t saturate for positive values (gradient = 1), enabling faster training and mitigating vanishing gradients. It also introduces sparsity, which may help with feature selection.



1.3.3 Dropout Regularization
Motivation: Neural networks with large capacity tend to overfit training data. Dropout provides an efficient regularization mechanism by preventing co-adaptation of neurons.
Training Phase: For each mini-batch, randomly set activation outputs to zero with probability \(1 - p_{\text{keep}}\):
\[\mathbf{a}_{\text{dropout}} = \mathbf{m} \odot \mathbf{a} \cdot \frac{1}{p_{\text{keep}}}\]
where:

\(\mathbf{m} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_{\text{keep}})\) is a binary mask
\(\odot\) denotes element-wise multiplication
The scaling factor \(1/p_{\text{keep}}\) maintains expected activation magnitude

Inference Phase: Use all neurons without dropout (\(\mathbf{a}_{\text{test}} = \mathbf{a}\)). The training-time scaling ensures test-time expectations match.
Intuition: Dropout can be viewed as:

Implicit Ensemble: Training an exponential number of sub-networks that share parameters
Regularization: Prevents complex co-adaptations by forcing neurons to be robust individually

Typical Values: \(p_{\text{keep}} \in [0.5, 0.8]\) for hidden layers; often \(p_{\text{keep}} = 1.0\) (no dropout) for input/output layers.
Interview Note: Modern architectures (especially Transformers) often use dropout sparingly or replace it with other regularization (weight decay, layer normalization). Be ready to discuss this trend.



1.3.4 Normalization Techniques

1.3.4.1 Batch Normalization
Motivation: During training, the distribution of inputs to each layer changes as parameters update (internal covariate shift). This forces layers to continuously adapt, slowing convergence. Batch Normalization stabilizes these distributions.
Algorithm (applied per mini-batch):
Given a mini-batch \(\mathcal{B} = \{\mathbf{z}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{z}^{(B)}\}\) where \(\mathbf{z}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^d\):

Compute statistics per dimension \(j = 1, \ldots, d\): \[\mu_j = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B z_j^{(i)}\] \[\sigma_j^2 = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B (z_j^{(i)} - \mu_j)^2\]
Normalize: \[\hat{z}_j^{(i)} = \frac{z_j^{(i)} - \mu_j}{\sqrt{\sigma_j^2 + \epsilon}}\]
where \(\epsilon \approx 10^{-5}\) prevents division by zero
Scale and shift (learnable parameters): \[y_j^{(i)} = \gamma_j \hat{z}_j^{(i)} + \beta_j\]

Parameters: Each dimension has learnable \(\gamma_j\) (scale) and \(\beta_j\) (shift). This allows the network to undo normalization if beneficial.
Inference: Use running averages of \(\mu_j\) and \(\sigma_j^2\) computed during training: \[\mu_{\text{running}} \leftarrow \alpha \mu_{\text{running}} + (1-\alpha) \mu_{\text{batch}}\] \[\sigma^2_{\text{running}} \leftarrow \alpha \sigma^2_{\text{running}} + (1-\alpha) \sigma^2_{\text{batch}}\]
where \(\alpha \approx 0.9\) is the momentum parameter.
Placement: Typically applied before activation functions (though after activation is also used): \[\mathbf{y} = \text{Activation}(\text{BatchNorm}(\mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}))\]
Benefits:

Enables higher learning rates (gradients don’t explode/vanish as easily)
Acts as regularizer (each sample sees different normalizations due to batch sampling)
Reduces sensitivity to initialization

Numpy Implementation (forward pass only):
def batch_norm_forward(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    """
    x: (N, D) input
    gamma, beta: (D,) scale and shift parameters
    """
    # Compute statistics
    mu = np.mean(x, axis=0)  # (D,)
    var = np.var(x, axis=0)  # (D,)
    
    # Normalize
    x_normalized = (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps)
    
    # Scale and shift
    out = gamma * x_normalized + beta
    
    # Cache for backward pass
    cache = (x, x_normalized, mu, var, gamma, beta, eps)
    return out, cache
Interview Deep-Dive: Be ready to explain:

Why running statistics are needed at test time (batch size = 1)
Why BatchNorm breaks in small batches or sequence models (→ LayerNorm)
The controversy around “internal covariate shift” vs. just smoothing loss landscape




1.3.4.2 Normalization Variants for Images
For convolutional networks with spatial dimensions, different normalization strategies are used:








Method
Normalization Axes
Use Case




Batch Norm
\((N, H, W)\) per channel
Standard CNNs with moderate batch size


Layer Norm
\((C, H, W)\) per sample
Small batches, sequence models


Instance Norm

Style transfer, GANs


Group Norm
Groups of channels \((G, H, W)\)
Very small batches



Tensor Notation: For input \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C \times H \times W}\):

\(N\) = batch size
\(C\) = channels
\(H, W\) = spatial dimensions

BatchNorm2D: Normalize across \((N, H, W)\) for each channel \(c\): \[\hat{x}_{n,c,h,w} = \frac{x_{n,c,h,w} - \mu_c}{\sqrt{\sigma_c^2 + \epsilon}}\] where \(\mu_c, \sigma_c^2\) are computed over all \(N \times H \times W\) spatial positions.
LayerNorm: Normalize across \((C, H, W)\) for each sample \(n\): \[\hat{x}_{n,c,h,w} = \frac{x_{n,c,h,w} - \mu_n}{\sqrt{\sigma_n^2 + \epsilon}}\]
Why LayerNorm for Transformers? Sequence lengths vary, making batch statistics unstable. LayerNorm computes statistics per sample, avoiding this issue. It’s now standard in Transformers (BERT, GPT, ViT).

title: 1  Neural Networks and Optimization
text:
1.4 Loss Functions

1.4.1 Binary Classification
Logistic Regression Model: \[\hat{y} = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b), \quad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\]
Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) Loss: \[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \left[ y_i \log \hat{y}_i + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - \hat{y}_i) \right]\]
where \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\) is the ground truth label.
Probabilistic Interpretation:

Minimizing BCE is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) under Bernoulli distribution
\(\hat{y}_i\) represents \(P(y=1 | \mathbf{x}_i; \theta)\)

Gradient (for single example): \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{w}} = (\hat{y} - y) \mathbf{x}\]
This clean gradient is why we use log loss (the exponentials cancel nicely).



1.4.2 Multi-Class Classification
Softmax Function: For logits \(\mathbf{z} = [z_1, \ldots, z_K]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^K\), the softmax produces a probability distribution:
\[\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}}\]
Properties:

\(\sum_{k=1}^K \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k = 1\) (valid probability distribution)
Translation invariant: \(\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z} + c) = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})\) for constant \(c\)
Smooth approximation to argmax (approaches one-hot as temperature \(\rightarrow 0\))

Temperature Scaling: \[\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}/T)_k = \frac{e^{z_k/T}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j/T}}\]

\(T > 1\): Softer distribution (less confident)
\(T < 1\): Sharper distribution (more confident)

Categorical Cross-Entropy (CCE) Loss: \[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{k=1}^K y_{i,k} \log \hat{y}_{i,k}\]
where:

\(\mathbf{y}_i \in \{0,1\}^K\) is the one-hot encoded label
\(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_i)\) is the predicted probability

Simplified Form (since only one \(y_{i,k} = 1\)): \[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \log \hat{y}_{i, c_i}\]
where \(c_i\) is the true class index for example \(i\).
Numerical Stability: Compute log-softmax directly to avoid overflow: \[\log \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k = z_k - \log \sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}\]
Interview Question: “Why not use MSE for classification?” Answer: MSE assumes Gaussian likelihood, inappropriate for discrete labels. Cross-entropy corresponds to the correct likelihood (categorical distribution) and provides better gradients for probability outputs.



1.4.3 Regression Tasks
Mean Squared Error (MSE): \[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^m \|\mathbf{y}_i - \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\|^2\]
Equivalent to MLE under Gaussian noise: \(y = f_\theta(\mathbf{x}) + \epsilon\), where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\).
Mean Absolute Error (MAE): \[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m |\mathbf{y}_i - \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i|\]
More robust to outliers than MSE (Laplace likelihood).
Huber Loss (smooth combination): \[\mathcal{L}_\delta(y, \hat{y}) = \begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2}(y - \hat{y})^2 & \text{if } |y - \hat{y}| \leq \delta \\
\delta |y - \hat{y}| - \frac{1}{2}\delta^2 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}\]
Quadratic for small errors (smooth gradients), linear for large errors (outlier robustness).

title: 1  Neural Networks and Optimization
text:
1.5 Backpropagation
Fundamental Principle: Backpropagation efficiently computes gradients of the loss with respect to all parameters using the chain rule of calculus.

1.5.1 Chain Rule Foundation
For composed functions \(z = f(y)\) and \(y = g(x)\):
\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\]
In neural networks, each layer is a function \(\mathbf{z}^{[\ell+1]} = f^{[\ell]}(\mathbf{z}^{[\ell]}, \mathbf{W}^{[\ell]}, \mathbf{b}^{[\ell]})\).
Forward Pass: Compute activations sequentially:
\[\mathbf{z}^{[0]} = \mathbf{x}\] \[\mathbf{z}^{[\ell+1]} = \sigma^{[\ell]}(\mathbf{W}^{[\ell]} \mathbf{z}^{[\ell]} + \mathbf{b}^{[\ell]})\] \[\hat{y} = \mathbf{z}^{[L]}\]
Backward Pass: Compute gradients recursively from output to input.


1.5.2 Gradient Computation
Define the error signal at layer \(\ell\): \[\boldsymbol{\delta}^{[\ell]} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{[\ell]}}\]
Recursive Formula (chain rule): \[\boldsymbol{\delta}^{[\ell]} = \left(\mathbf{W}^{[\ell]}\right)^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}^{[\ell+1]} \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{[\ell]})\]
where \(\odot\) is element-wise multiplication and \(\sigma'\) is the derivative of the activation.
Parameter Gradients:
\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{[\ell]}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{[\ell+1]} \left(\mathbf{z}^{[\ell]}\right)^\top\] \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{[\ell]}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{[\ell+1]}\]


1.5.3 Computational Efficiency
Why Backpropagation?

Naively computing \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) using finite differences requires \(O(|\theta|)\) forward passes
Backpropagation computes all gradients in one forward + one backward pass
Time complexity: \(O(W)\) where \(W\) is the number of edges in the computational graph

Memory Optimization:

Storing all intermediate activations for backward pass requires \(O(L \cdot d)\) memory
Gradient checkpointing trades computation for memory: recompute activations during backward pass

Interview Insight: Modern frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) use automatic differentiation (autograd) which generalizes backpropagation to arbitrary computation graphs. Understanding the chain rule is essential for debugging gradient flow issues.

title: 1  Neural Networks and Optimization
text:
1.6 Optimization Algorithms

1.6.1 Gradient Descent Variants
Core Update Rule: \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \alpha \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\]
where \(\alpha > 0\) is the learning rate.
Three Flavors:

Batch Gradient Descent: Compute loss over entire dataset

Accurate gradient estimates
Slow and memory-intensive for large datasets

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD): Use one sample at a time

Fast updates
High variance in gradient estimates
Can escape shallow local minima (noise helps exploration)

Mini-Batch Gradient Descent: Use batch of \(B\) samples (typically \(B \in [32, 512]\))

Standard choice in practice
Balances gradient accuracy and computational efficiency
Batch size affects generalization (smaller often better)


Why Mini-Batches Work:

Vectorized operations on GPUs/TPUs are efficient
Stochasticity helps escape sharp minima (which generalize poorly)
Effective batch size can be increased via gradient accumulation




1.6.2 Momentum-Based Methods
SGD with Momentum: \[\mathbf{v}_{t+1} = \beta \mathbf{v}_t + (1-\beta) \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\] \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \alpha \mathbf{v}_{t+1}\]
where \(\beta \in [0, 1)\) is the momentum coefficient (typically \(\beta = 0.9\)).
Intuition: - Gradient is a noisy estimate of the true descent direction - Momentum accumulates an exponentially weighted moving average - Acts like a “heavy ball” rolling downhill—builds velocity in consistent directions, dampens oscillations
Benefits:

Accelerates convergence in directions of low curvature
Reduces oscillations in directions of high curvature
Can pass through small barriers in loss landscape

Physical Analogy: Consider optimizing on a ravine:

Pure SGD oscillates across narrow dimension
Momentum dampens oscillations while accelerating along the ravine




1.6.3 Adaptive Learning Rates
Motivation: The loss landscape is often ill-conditioned—curvature varies dramatically across parameter dimensions. A single global learning rate is inefficient:

Too large → oscillates in steep directions
Too small → slow progress in flat directions

Ideal Solution: Newton’s Method uses the Hessian \(\mathbf{H}\) (second derivatives): \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \alpha \mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\]
This normalizes by curvature, but computing/inverting \(\mathbf{H}\) is prohibitively expensive for high-dimensional \(\theta\).
Practical Approach: Approximate the diagonal of the inverse Hessian using gradient statistics.


1.6.3.1 RMSProp
Algorithm: \[\mathbf{v}_t = \beta \mathbf{v}_{t-1} + (1-\beta) \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)^2\] \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{\mathbf{v}_t + \epsilon}} \odot \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\]
where:

\(\mathbf{v}_t\) is the moving average of squared gradients (element-wise)
\(\epsilon \approx 10^{-8}\) prevents division by zero
\(\beta \approx 0.9\) is the decay rate

Intuition:

Parameters with consistently large gradients get smaller effective learning rates
Parameters with small gradients get larger effective learning rates
Approximates diagonal Hessian via \(\mathbb{E}[g^2] \approx \text{diag}(\mathbf{H})\) when loss is quadratic




1.6.3.2 Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation)
Algorithm: Combines momentum (first moment) and RMSProp (second moment):
\[\mathbf{m}_t = \beta_1 \mathbf{m}_{t-1} + (1-\beta_1) \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\] \[\mathbf{v}_t = \beta_2 \mathbf{v}_{t-1} + (1-\beta_2) \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)^2\]
Bias Correction (important for early iterations): \[\hat{\mathbf{m}}_t = \frac{\mathbf{m}_t}{1 - \beta_1^t}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{v}}_t = \frac{\mathbf{v}_t}{1 - \beta_2^t}\]
Update: \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_t} + \epsilon} \odot \hat{\mathbf{m}}_t\]
Hyperparameters (standard defaults):

\(\beta_1 = 0.9\) (momentum)
\(\beta_2 = 0.999\) (RMSProp decay)
\(\alpha = 0.001\) (learning rate)
\(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\)

Why Bias Correction?

\(\mathbf{m}_0 = \mathbf{v}_0 = \mathbf{0}\) → biased toward zero initially
Correction factors \((1-\beta^t)^{-1}\) compensate for this initialization bias
Becomes negligible for large \(t\)

Adam vs. SGD Trade-off:

Adam: Faster initial convergence, less sensitive to learning rate
SGD+Momentum: Often better final generalization (especially in vision)
Current research: AdamW (Adam with decoupled weight decay) bridges this gap

Interview Question: “When would you choose Adam over SGD?” Answer: Adam for fast prototyping, non-stationary problems, and when tuning learning rate is difficult. SGD+momentum when generalization is critical and you have time for hyperparameter search. Transformers typically use Adam/AdamW.




1.6.4 Learning Rate Schedules
Motivation: Fixed learning rates are suboptimal: - Early training: Large LR for fast progress - Late training: Small LR for fine-tuning
Common Schedules:

Step Decay: \[\alpha_t = \alpha_0 \cdot \gamma^{\lfloor t/s \rfloor}\] Drop LR by factor \(\gamma\) every \(s\) epochs (e.g., \(\gamma=0.1\), \(s=30\))
Exponential Decay: \[\alpha_t = \alpha_0 \cdot e^{-\lambda t}\]
Cosine Annealing: \[\alpha_t = \alpha_{\min} + \frac{1}{2}(\alpha_{\max} - \alpha_{\min})(1 + \cos(\pi t/T))\] Smooth decay to \(\alpha_{\min}\) over \(T\) iterations
Warmup: \[\alpha_t = \alpha_{\text{max}} \cdot \min\left(1, \frac{t}{T_{\text{warmup}}}\right)\] Linear increase for first \(T_{\text{warmup}}\) steps
Why? Large initial learning rates can destabilize training when parameters are random. Warmup is especially important for Transformers.
One-Cycle:

Increase LR from \(\alpha_{\text{min}}\) to \(\alpha_{\text{max}}\) (30% of training)
Decrease LR back to \(\alpha_{\text{min}}\) (70% of training)
Popular for fast convergence in limited-budget scenarios


Practical Advice:

ResNets: Step decay at epochs 30, 60, 90
Transformers: Warmup + cosine or inverse square root decay
Try adaptive schedules (ReduceLROnPlateau) when validation loss plateaus

title: 1  Neural Networks and Optimization
text:
1.7 Generalization and Regularization

1.7.1 Train/Validation/Test Split
Standard Practice:

Training set (70-80%): Optimize model parameters \(\theta\)
Validation set (10-15%): Select hyperparameters, early stopping
Test set (10-15%): Report final performance (use only once!)

Why Three Splits?

Validation performance guides model selection → introduces bias
Test set remains untouched until final evaluation → unbiased performance estimate

Cross-Validation: When data is limited, use \(k\)-fold CV on train+validation, reserve test set for final evaluation only.

title: 2  Generalization and Learning Theory
text:
2.1 Bias-Variance Tradeoff
Definitions:
Decomposition (for squared loss): \[\mathbb{E}[(y - \hat{y})^2] = \text{Bias}[\hat{y}]^2 + \text{Var}[\hat{y}] + \text{Noise}\]
Identifying Issues:
Modern Deep Learning Paradox:
Interview Insight: Be prepared to discuss why deep learning defies classical bias-variance intuition. Theories include implicit regularization from SGD, the “lottery ticket hypothesis,” and interpolation vs. extrapolation regimes.

title: 2  Generalization and Learning Theory
text:
Bias: Error from incorrect assumptions (e.g., linear model for nonlinear data)
Variance: Error from sensitivity to training set fluctuations




High Bias (underfitting):

Train error >> human-level performance
Train error ≈ validation error (both high)
Solutions: Increase model capacity, train longer, reduce regularization

High Variance (overfitting):

Train error << validation error (large gap)
Train error ≈ human-level performance
Solutions: More data, regularization, simpler model




Classical theory: Larger models should overfit more
Reality: Over-parameterized networks often generalize better
Double Descent: Test error initially increases with model size (classical regime), then decreases again (modern regime)

title: 2  Generalization and Learning Theory
text:
2.2 Regularization Techniques

2.2.1 L2 Regularization (Weight Decay)
Modified Loss: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \|\mathbf{W}\|_F^2\]
where \(\|\mathbf{W}\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{ij} W_{ij}^2}\) is the Frobenius norm.
Update Rule: \[\mathbf{W}_{t+1} = \mathbf{W}_t - \alpha(\nabla_W \mathcal{L} + \lambda \mathbf{W}_t) = (1-\alpha\lambda)\mathbf{W}_t - \alpha \nabla_W \mathcal{L}\]
Effect: Shrinks weights toward zero each step (“weight decay”). Equivalent to MAP estimation with Gaussian prior on weights.
Typical Values: \(\lambda \in [10^{-5}, 10^{-3}]\)



2.2.2 L1 Regularization (Lasso)
Modified Loss: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \lambda \|\mathbf{W}\|_1\]
where \(\|\mathbf{W}\|_1 = \sum_{ij} |W_{ij}|\).
Effect: Promotes sparsity (many weights exactly zero). Equivalent to MAP with Laplace prior.
Use Case: Feature selection, interpretability, model compression.



2.2.3 Dropout (Covered in §1.2.3)
Additional Perspective: Dropout can be viewed as a form of Bayesian approximation—training stochastic sub-networks approximates integrating over model uncertainty.



2.2.4 Data Augmentation
Definition: Apply label-preserving transformations to training data: - Vision: Rotation, flipping, cropping, color jittering, mixup - NLP: Synonym replacement, back-translation, word dropout - Audio: Time stretching, pitch shifting, noise injection
Why It Works: - Increases effective dataset size - Encodes domain-specific invariances (e.g., object recognition should be translation-invariant)
Practical Note: Augmentation is the most important regularization for vision tasks. Allocate effort here before tuning other hyperparameters.



2.2.5 Label Smoothing
Motivation: Hard labels (one-hot vectors) encourage overconfident predictions. Models can achieve zero cross-entropy loss by outputting extreme logits, which hurts calibration.
Method: Replace \(y \in \{0,1\}^K\) with: \[\tilde{y}_k = \begin{cases}
1 - \epsilon & \text{if } k = c \text{ (true class)} \\
\epsilon / (K-1) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}\]
where \(\epsilon \in [0.1, 0.2]\) is the smoothing parameter.
Effect: - Prevents model from becoming too confident - Improves calibration (predicted probabilities match true frequencies) - Acts as implicit regularization



2.2.6 Early Stopping
Algorithm: 1. Monitor validation loss every epoch 2. Stop training when validation loss hasn’t improved for \(n\) epochs (patience) 3. Restore weights from best validation epoch
Intuition: Validation loss initially decreases with training loss, then starts increasing (overfitting). Early stopping finds the “sweet spot.”
Criticism: Couples optimization (minimizing training loss) with regularization (preventing overfitting). Modern practice prefers explicit regularization + training to convergence.
When to Use: Quick experiments, when computational budget is limited, or when other regularization is insufficient.



2.2.7 Model Ensembles
Definition: Train multiple models independently and average predictions: \[\hat{y}_{\text{ensemble}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^M \hat{y}^{(i)}\]
Variants:

Different random initializations
Different architectures
Different hyperparameters
Different data subsets (bagging)

Why It Works:

Reduces variance (errors of individual models are partially uncorrelated)
Can reduce bias if models are diverse
Almost always improves performance (at cost of \(M\times\) compute)

Practical Use:

Kaggle competitions (critical for winning)
Production systems where performance is crucial
Not suitable for real-time or resource-constrained applications

title: 2  Generalization and Learning Theory
text:
2.3 Understanding Overfitting Mechanisms
Classical View: Overfitting occurs when models learn noise rather than signal. However, modern deep learning reveals this intuition is incomplete—we need to understand how and why networks overfit.

2.3.1 Capacity and Memorization
VC Dimension: The largest number of points a model can perfectly classify for all possible labelings. For neural networks:

Linear classifier in \(\mathbb{R}^d\): \(\text{VC} = d + 1\)
Two-layer ReLU network: \(\text{VC} = O(W^2)\) where \(W\) is total parameters

Empirical Finding (Zhang et al., 2017): Neural networks can perfectly fit random labels—demonstrating they have capacity to memorize. Yet on real data, they prefer to learn patterns first.
Rademacher Complexity: A data-dependent capacity measure that predicts generalization better than parameter count alone. For dataset \(\mathcal{S}\):
\[\hat{\mathcal{R}}_\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} \left[ \sup_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma_i h(\mathbf{x}_i) \right]\]
where \(\sigma_i \in \{-1, +1\}\) are random labels. Higher complexity → can fit random noise → higher overfitting risk.



2.3.2 Sharp vs. Flat Minima
Loss Landscape Geometry: Not all zero-training-loss solutions generalize equally.

Sharp minimum: Small weight perturbations cause large loss increase
Flat minimum: Loss remains stable under perturbations

Connection to Generalization (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997): Flat minima generalize better because they occupy larger volumes in parameter space—a form of Occam’s razor.
Why SGD Finds Flat Minima:

Large batch → converges to sharp minima → poor generalization
Small batch → noisy gradients → flat minima → better generalization

The noise in mini-batch SGD acts as implicit regularization, preventing convergence to sharp, overfitting solutions.
Practical Implication: Batch size affects generalization not just through gradient estimation, but through the geometry of the solutions found.



2.3.3 Implicit Regularization from Optimization
Key Insight: The optimization algorithm itself regularizes, beyond explicit terms in the loss.
Evidence: 1. Max-Margin Solutions (Soudry et al., 2018): For separable data, gradient descent on cross-entropy converges to the maximum-margin classifier (SVM solution), even without explicit margin maximization.

Simplicity Bias: SGD learns low-frequency patterns before high-frequency noise. This can be formalized via Neural Tangent Kernel theory—networks learn functions in order of increasing NTK eigenvalues.
Early Stopping Exploits This: Stopping before complete interpolation retains learned structure while discarding noise.

Interview Insight: When asked “Why do large networks generalize?”, mention multiple mechanisms working together: implicit regularization from SGD, architecture inductive biases, flat minima preference, and simplicity bias. No single explanation is complete.

title: 2  Generalization and Learning Theory
text:
2.4 Modern Generalization Puzzles
Classical theory predicts that over-parameterized models should catastrophically overfit. Reality contradicts this. Understanding these paradoxes is essential for modern deep learning research.

2.4.1 Double Descent Phenomenon
Discovery (Belkin et al., 2019; Nakkiran et al., 2020): Test error follows a double descent curve rather than the classical U-shape:
Test Error
    ^
    |   Classical  | Modern
    |    Regime    | Regime
    |              |
    |   ∩         ∩|
    |  / \       / |
    | /   \_____/  |
    |______________|_____> Model Capacity
           ↑
    Interpolation
     Threshold
Three Regimes:

Under-parameterized (\(\mathcal{C} < \mathcal{C}_{\text{interp}}\)): Classical U-curve—insufficient capacity forces generalization
Interpolation threshold (\(\mathcal{C} \approx \mathcal{C}_{\text{interp}}\)): Peak test error—forced to fit noise with high-frequency components
Over-parameterized (\(\mathcal{C} > \mathcal{C}_{\text{interp}}\)): Test error decreases—multiple interpolating solutions exist, optimization finds simpler ones

Why This Occurs: When many solutions achieve zero training loss, gradient descent converges to the minimum-norm solution. In high dimensions, this tends to be smoother and generalizes better.
Practical Implications:

More parameters can improve generalization (beyond classical intuition)
Regularization can worsen performance at interpolation threshold (reduces effective capacity)
Modern LLMs operate deep in over-parameterized regime (GPT-3: 175B parameters)

Interview Question: “Should we worry about overfitting with billion-parameter models?”
Answer: Depends on regime. If \(|\theta| \gg |\mathcal{D}|\), we’re over-parameterized where implicit regularization dominates. Still need sufficient data for task complexity and proper optimization.



2.4.2 The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
Statement (Frankle & Carlin, 2019): > A randomly-initialized dense network contains a sparse subnetwork that—when trained in isolation with its original initialization—matches the full network’s test accuracy.
Formal Definition: Given network with initialization \(\theta_0\), there exists a binary mask \(\mathbf{m} \in \{0,1\}^{|\theta|}\) such that:
\[f(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{m} \odot \theta_0) \text{ trained achieves similar accuracy as } f(\mathbf{x}; \theta_0)\]
where \(||\mathbf{m}||_0 \ll |\theta|\) (e.g., 10-20% of weights).
Key Insight: The specific initialization matters as much as architecture—winning tickets exist in the initialization lottery.
Finding Tickets - Iterative Magnitude Pruning:

Train network: \(\theta_0 \rightarrow \theta_T\)
Prune smallest magnitude weights by \(|\theta_{T,i}|\)
Reset remaining weights to \(\theta_0\) (not re-randomize)
Repeat

Crucially: Must reset to original \(\theta_0\)—this specific initialization is the “ticket.”
Theoretical Implications:

Over-parameterization as search space: Large networks contain more potential tickets
Initialization contains seeds: Training reveals which subset of initial weights to use
Connection to optimization: SGD searches over exponentially many subnetworks implicitly

Weak Lottery Tickets (Frankle et al., 2020): For large-scale networks, must reset to \(\theta_k\) (after \(k\) early epochs) instead of \(\theta_0\) for stability. Enables lottery tickets in ResNets, Transformers.
Practical Applications:

Model compression: Train large → find ticket → deploy small
Training efficiency: Prune early, continue training pruned network
Understanding hyperparameters: Learning rate, batch size affect which ticket is found

Open Questions:

Theoretical conditions guaranteeing ticket existence?
Connection to double descent and implicit regularization?
Universal tickets that transfer across tasks?

Interview Insight: Lottery tickets explain why over-parameterization helps: more parameters → more diverse subnetworks → higher probability of finding good solutions. Connects initialization, architecture, and optimization.

Synthesis: Modern generalization is explained by multiple interacting phenomena:

Double descent: Over-parameterization enables simpler interpolating solutions
Lottery tickets: Initialization space contains rare good subnetworks
Implicit regularization: SGD bias toward flat minima and simple solutions
Architecture biases: Convolutions, attention impose structured priors

Understanding these mechanisms is essential for designing scalable deep learning systems and explains why practices like massive over-parameterization and careful initialization matter in production.

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
3.1 Motivation and Inductive Biases
Why CNNs for Images? Fully-connected networks treat each pixel independently, ignoring spatial structure. For a 224×224 RGB image, the first layer alone would require ~150K weights per neuron—leading to overfitting and computational infeasibility.
Key Inductive Biases:
CNNs encode these biases through local connectivity (receptive fields), weight sharing (same filter across spatial locations), and hierarchical stacking (deeper layers see larger regions).

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Locality: Nearby pixels are more related than distant ones
Translation Equivariance: Objects can appear anywhere in the image
Hierarchical Composition: Low-level edges → mid-level textures → high-level objects

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
3.2 Convolutional Layers

3.2.1 Standard Convolution
Definition: A convolutional layer applies a learnable filter (kernel) \(\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k \times c_{\text{in}}}\) to an input tensor \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times c_{\text{in}}}\) via discrete convolution (technically cross-correlation):
\[\mathbf{Y}[i,j,c_{\text{out}}] = \sum_{c=1}^{c_{\text{in}}} \sum_{p=0}^{k-1} \sum_{q=0}^{k-1} \mathbf{X}[i+p, j+q, c] \cdot \mathbf{K}[p,q,c,c_{\text{out}}] + b_{c_{\text{out}}}\]
where \(\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{h' \times w' \times c_{\text{out}}}\) is the output.
Below is an animation illustrating how a standard convolution kernel slides across the input and produces feature activations.



Animation of a standard 2D convolution. A kernel scans the input spatially, computing weighted sums at each position to produce the output feature map. Adapted from Dumoulin and Visin (Dumoulin and Visin 2016).


Key Hyperparameters:








Parameter
Description
Typical Values




Kernel size \(k\)
Receptive field dimension
3×3 (most common), 5×5, 7×7


Stride \(s\)
Step size when sliding filter
1 (default), 2 (downsampling)


Padding \(p\)
Border handling
0 (‘valid’), \((k-1)/2\) (‘same’)


Input channels \(c_{\text{in}}\)
Depth of input
3 (RGB), 64, 128, …


Output channels \(c_{\text{out}}\)
Number of filters
64, 128, 256, 512



 Output Spatial Dimensions: \[h' = \left\lfloor \frac{h + 2p - k}{s} \right\rfloor + 1, \quad w' = \left\lfloor \frac{w + 2p - k}{s} \right\rfloor + 1\]
Parameter Count: \(k \times k \times c_{\text{in}} \times c_{\text{out}} + c_{\text{out}}\) (weights + biases)
Example: A 3×3 conv with \(c_{\text{in}}=64\), \(c_{\text{out}}=128\) has \(3 \times 3 \times 64 \times 128 + 128 = 73{,}856\) parameters.
Translation Equivariance: If input \(\mathbf{X}\) is shifted by \((dx, dy)\), output \(\mathbf{Y}\) shifts by \((dx/s, dy/s)\): \[\text{Conv}(\text{Shift}(\mathbf{X})) = \text{Shift}(\text{Conv}(\mathbf{X}))\]
This property is critical for object detection—detecting a car at different locations uses the same learned features.



3.2.2 Dilated Convolutions
Also called Atrous Convolutions, or Convolution with Holes.
Definition: Insert zeros (holes) between kernel elements to increase receptive field without adding parameters:
\[\mathbf{Y}[i,j] = \sum_{p,q} \mathbf{X}[i + r \cdot p, j + r \cdot q] \cdot \mathbf{K}[p,q]\]
where \(r\) is the dilation rate.



Dilated convolution (atrous convolution). The kernel uses spaced sampling points, expanding receptive field without increasing parameters. (Dumoulin and Visin 2016)


Effective Receptive Field:

Standard 3×3: covers 3×3 region
Dilated 3×3 with \(r=2\): covers 5×5 region
Dilated 3×3 with \(r=3\): covers 7×7 region

Applications:

Semantic Segmentation (DeepLab): Maintain spatial resolution while expanding receptive field
Audio (WaveNet): Exponentially growing receptive fields (\(r = 2^{\ell}\) at layer \(\ell\))

Interview Insight: “Why dilated convolutions in segmentation?” Answer: Pooling reduces resolution (bad for dense prediction). Dilated convs increase receptive field without losing spatial detail.



3.2.3 Deformable Convolutions
Standard convolutions use fixed sampling grids. Deformable convolutions learn adaptive sampling locations, allowing receptive fields to deform based on image content.
Definition: Augment standard convolution with learnable 2D offsets \(\{\Delta p_n\}\):
\[\mathbf{Y}[i,j] = \sum_{p_n \in \mathcal{R}}  \mathbf{X}[i + p_n + \Delta p_n] \cdot \mathbf{K}[p_n] \]
where \(\Delta p_n = (\Delta x_n, \Delta y_n)\) is the learned offset for location \(p_n\) in the grid \(\mathcal{R}\).
Mechanism: A parallel convolution predicts \(2k^2\) offsets (x,y for each kernel position), then the main convolution samples from these deformed locations (using bilinear interpolation for fractional offsets).



Deformable convolution with learned offsets. The network predicts spatial offsets for each sampling position, allowing the receptive field to adapt to object geometry. (Dai et al. 2017)


Key Advantages:

Receptive field adapts to object scale/shape—thin objects get elongated fields, large objects get expanded fields—all learned automatically.
Unlike Dilated Convolutions, which use fixed sparse sampling,
Deformable Convolutions learn where to sample (content-adaptive), with minimal parameter overhead (~1 extra conv layer for offset prediction).

Applications: Object detection (Deformable DETR); semantic segmentation (better boundaries); video modeling (motion adaptation).



3.2.4 Transposed Convolutions
Also called Deconvolutions.
Purpose: Upsample spatial dimensions—opposite of standard convolution.
Mechanism:

Insert zeros between input pixels (dilate input by stride \(s\))
Apply standard convolution with stride 1




Transposed convolution. The operation expands spatial resolution by reversing the geometry of strided convolution, commonly used in decoders and generative models. Adapted from Dumoulin and Visin (Dumoulin and Visin 2016).


Output Size: For input \(h \times w\), kernel \(k\), stride \(s\), padding \(p\): \[h_{\text{out}} = s \cdot (h-1) + k - 2p\]
Checkerboard Artifacts: Overlapping receptive fields cause uneven coverage.
Solution: Use \(k\) divisible by \(s\), or replace with Upsample + Conv:
nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2, mode='bilinear')
nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
Applications: U-Net decoder, GAN generators, semantic segmentation upsampling.



3.2.5 Depthwise Separable Convolutions
Motivation: Standard convolutions are expensive. For input \(h \times w \times c_{\text{in}}\) and output \(h \times w \times c_{\text{out}}\):

Standard: \(k^2 \cdot c_{\text{in}} \cdot c_{\text{out}} \cdot h \cdot w\) operations
Depthwise Separable: Factorize into two steps

Algorithm:

Depthwise Convolution: Apply one \(k \times k\) filter per input channel \[\mathbf{Z}[i,j,c] = \sum_{p,q} \mathbf{X}[i+p,j+q,c] \cdot \mathbf{K}_{\text{depth}}[p,q,c]\] Output: \(h \times w \times c_{\text{in}}\) (same channels)
Pointwise Convolution: 1×1 conv to mix channels \[\mathbf{Y}[i,j,c_{\text{out}}] = \sum_{c=1}^{c_{\text{in}}} \mathbf{Z}[i,j,c] \cdot \mathbf{K}_{\text{point}}[c, c_{\text{out}}]\] Output: \(h \times w \times c_{\text{out}}\)

The following illustration shows the two steps of a separable convolution.












Figure 3.1: Depthwise separable convolution.
Left: Depthwise convolution applies one spatial filter per input channel.
Right: Pointwise \(1 \times 1\) convolution mixes channel information. This factorization drastically reduces computation while preserving expressiveness (used in MobileNet). Image source: (Wang 2018)



Complexity Reduction: \[\frac{\text{Depthwise Sep}}{\text{Standard}} = \frac{k^2 \cdot c_{\text{in}} + c_{\text{in}} \cdot c_{\text{out}}}{k^2 \cdot c_{\text{in}} \cdot c_{\text{out}}} = \frac{1}{c_{\text{out}}} + \frac{1}{k^2}\]
For \(k=3\), \(c_{\text{out}}=128\): ~8-9× fewer parameters with minimal accuracy loss.
Use Cases: MobileNets; EfficientNets (mobile/edge deployment); Xception (competitive with ResNet at lower cost).

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
3.3 Pooling and Downsampling
Pooling Layers: Reduce spatial dimensions while retaining important features.
Unlike convolutions, pooling is a channel-wise, non-learnable operation.
Max Pooling: \[\mathbf{Y}[i,j,c] = \max_{p,q \in \text{Window}} \mathbf{X}[si + p, sj + q, c]\]

Retains strongest activations (preserves edges/features)
Non-differentiable at non-max locations (subgradients used in backprop)




Max pooling operation. A downsampling layer that selects the maximum value in each region, reducing spatial resolution while preserving dominant features. (Dumoulin and Visin 2016)


Average Pooling: \[\mathbf{Y}[i,j,c] = \frac{1}{k^2} \sum_{p,q \in \text{Window}} \mathbf{X}[si + p, sj + q, c]\]

Smoother downsampling
Less common in modern architectures

Global Average Pooling (GAP): \[\mathbf{Y}[c] = \frac{1}{h \cdot w} \sum_{i=1}^h \sum_{j=1}^w \mathbf{X}[i,j,c]\]

Reduces \(h \times w \times c\) to \(c\) (one value per channel)
Replaces fully-connected layers in ResNet, EfficientNet
Why? Fewer parameters, handles variable input sizes, acts as spatial regularization

Strided Convolutions: Modern alternative to pooling

Apply conv with stride \(s > 1\)
Learnable downsampling (vs. fixed max/average)
Used in ResNet variants, DenseNet

Trade-off: Pooling (parameter-free, channel-wise, translation-robust)
vs. Strided Conv (learnable, mixes channels, more flexible)

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
3.4 Upsampling Layers
Purpose: Increase spatial resolution for tasks requiring dense, high-resolution outputs:

Image reconstruction (autoencoders, super-resolution)
Semantic segmentation (pixel-level classification)
Saliency/attention maps (visualizing model focus)
Generative models (GANs, diffusion decoders)



3.4.1 Basic Interpolation Methods
Nearest-Neighbor and Bilinear Interpolation are simple upsampling techniques:

Replicate (NN) or interpolate (bilinear) pixel values
No learnable parameters (like pooling layers)
Fast but produce blocky (NN) or blurred (bilinear) outputs
Useful for quick prototyping but limited representation capacity

Transposed Convolutions overlapping receptive fields cause uneven pixel coverage.
This is the so-called Checkerboard Problem, for example using a 3×3 kernel with stride 2:

Center pixels covered 9×
Edge pixels covered 4×
Corner pixels covered 1×

Result: Visible checkerboard pattern in outputs (especially in GAN generators).

[NOTE] Standard strided convolutions also create checkerboard artifacts but on the layer gradients, during backpropagation. This is typically less problematic than forward-pass artifacts.




3.4.2 Learnable Upsampling
Recommended Approach: Upsample + Convolution.
Modern Standard:
nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2, mode='bilinear', align_corners=False)
nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
Why This Works:

Separates upsampling (fixed) from feature learning (learnable)
Uniform coverage → no checkerboard artifacts
More stable training than transposed convolutions

Practical use (U-Net Decoder):
class UpsampleBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_ch, out_ch):
        super().__init__()
        self.up = nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2, mode='bilinear')
        self.conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(in_ch, out_ch, 3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(out_ch),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        )
    
    def forward(self, x, skip=None):
        x = self.up(x)
        if skip is not None:
            x = torch.cat([x, skip], dim=1)
        return self.conv(x)
Interview Insight: “Why avoid transposed convolutions?” Answer: Checkerboard artifacts visible in generated images. Modern practice uses upsample + conv for cleaner outputs. Reference: Distill article on deconvolution artifacts.

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
3.5 Residual Connections
Problem: Training very deep networks (50+ layers) causes degradation—not overfitting, but training error increases with depth.
Hypothesis (He et al., 2015): Optimization difficulty—deep networks struggle to learn identity mappings when needed.


Solution - Residual Block: \[\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \{\mathbf{W}_i\}) + \mathbf{x}\]
where \(\mathcal{F}\) is a stack of conv layers (e.g. Conv-BN-ReLU).








Intuition:

Network learns residual \(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})\) (deviation from identity)
If identity is optimal, \(\mathcal{F}\) can learn to output zeros (easy)
Standard networks must learn identity via complex weight configurations (hard)

Implementation:
class ResidualBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(channels)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(channels)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        residual = x
        out = F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out))
        out += residual  # Skip connection
        out = F.relu(out)
        return out
When dimensions change: Use 1×1 conv projection: \[\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{W}_s \mathbf{x}\]
where \(\mathbf{W}_s\) adjusts channels or resolution.
Benefits:

Gradient Flow: Gradients bypass \(\mathcal{F}\) via skip connection → mitigates vanishing gradients
Ensemble View: Network behaves like ensemble of shorter paths
Enables Depth: ResNet-152 (152 layers) trains successfully

Interview Question: “Why do residual connections help?” Answer:

Optimization—easier to learn deviations from identity,

Gradient flow—skip connections provide direct path for gradients,

Implicit ensembling—exponentially many paths of different lengths.

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Image Classification Task
Task Definition: Given image \(\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}\), predict class label \(c \in \{1, \ldots, C\}\) with confidence \(p \in [0,1]\).
ImageNet Challenge: The canonical benchmark driving CNN architecture evolution:

ImageNet-1K (ILSVRC): 1.28M training images, 1000 classes
Top-1 Accuracy: \(\arg\max_c p(c|\mathbf{I})\) is correct class
Top-5 Accuracy: Correct class in top 5 predictions (easier metric)

Standard Pipeline:
Image (224×224×3) → CNN Backbone → Global Pooling 
                   → Fully Connected → Softmax → Class Probabilities
Data Preprocessing:

Normalization: Mean subtraction, standard deviation division (per channel)

ImageNet: \(\mu = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406]\), \(\sigma = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]\)

Resizing: Center crop 224×224 from 256×256 (inference)

Data Augmentation (training only):

Spatial: Random crops, horizontal flips, rotations (±15°)
Color: Brightness/contrast jittering, hue shifts, grayscale conversion
Advanced: Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, AutoAugment

Why Augmentation Matters: CNNs are data-hungry—augmentation acts as powerful regularization, often improving top-1 accuracy by 2-5% on ImageNet.
Evolution:

2012: AlexNet (60% top-1) → Deep learning breakthrough
2015: ResNet-152 (77% top-1) → Enabled ultra-deep networks
2021: ViT-Huge (88.5% top-1) → Transformers match/exceed CNNs

Interview Note: Classification is the foundation—architectures proven here (ResNet, EfficientNet) become standard backbones for detection, segmentation, and other downstream tasks.

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
3.6 CNNs: Classic Architectures

3.6.1 LeNet-5 (1998) - The Pioneer
Architecture: Conv(6) → Pool → Conv(16) → Pool → FC(120) → FC(84) → FC(10)
Historical Context:

First successful application of backprop to CNNs
Digit recognition (MNIST, postal codes)
~60K parameters (tiny by modern standards)

Legacy: Established conv-pool-fc pattern used for 15+ years.






Figure 3.2: LeNet-5 architecture overview. Image Source: (Ng 2015).






3.6.2 AlexNet (2012) - Deep Learning Renaissance
Architecture:

5 conv layers, 3 fc layers
60M parameters
First use of ReLU (vs. tanh/sigmoid)
Dropout for regularization
Data augmentation (crops, flips, color jittering)

Innovation - ReLU Activation: \[\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)\]
vs. Sigmoid \(\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})\):

No saturation for positive values (gradient = 1)
6× faster training convergence
Sparse activation (many zeros)

Impact:

Won ImageNet 2012 (15.3% error vs. 26.2% runner-up)
Triggered deep learning boom
Demonstrated GPU training feasibility

Interview Insight: “What made AlexNet revolutionary?” Answer:
(1) Scale—first deep CNN on ImageNet,
(2) ReLU—enabled training deeper networks,
(3) Engineering—GPU implementation, dropout, data augmentation at scale.






Figure 3.3: AlexNet architecture overview. Image Source: (Ng 2015).






3.6.3 VGG-16 (2014) - Simplicity and Depth
Design Philosophy:

Uniform architecture: only 3×3 convs, 2×2 max pooling
Deeper is better (16-19 layers)

Why 3×3?

Two 3×3 convs = 5×5 receptive field with fewer parameters
Three 3×3 convs = 7×7 receptive field
More non-linearities (ReLU after each conv)

Parameters: 138M (VGG-16)—very large by 2014 standards
Trade-off:

✓ Simple, uniform design
✓ Strong performance
✗ Memory intensive (13 conv layers × large feature maps)
✗ Many parameters in FC layers

Legacy: Showed depth matters, established 3×3 as standard kernel size.






Figure 3.4: VGG-16 architecture overview. Image Source: (Ng 2015).






3.6.4 ResNet (2015) - Enabling Ultra-Deep Networks
Variants: ResNet-18, 34, 50, 101, 152 (number = layers)
Architecture (ResNet-50):

Conv1 (7×7, stride 2)
MaxPool (3×3, stride 2)
4 “stages” of residual blocks

Stage 2: 3 blocks, 256 channels
Stage 3: 4 blocks, 512 channels
Stage 4: 6 blocks, 1024 channels
Stage 5: 3 blocks, 2048 channels

Global Average Pooling
FC (2048 → num_classes)







Figure 3.5: Resnet-50 architecture overview.



Bottleneck Block (ResNet-50+):
1×1 conv (reduce channels 4×) 
→ 3×3 conv 
→ 1×1 conv (expand channels 4×) 
→ Add skip connection
Why Bottleneck? Reduces computation:

Standard: \(3 \times 3 \times 256 \times 256 = 589{,}824\) ops
Bottleneck: \(1 \times 1 \times 256 \times 64 + 3 \times 3 \times 64 \times 64 + 1 \times 1 \times 64 \times 256 = 69{,}632\) ops

Impact:

ILSVRC 2015 winner (3.57% error)
Standard backbone for detection, segmentation
Demonstrated 1000+ layer networks are possible




3.6.5 Inception (GoogLeNet, 2014)
Key Idea: Use multiple kernel sizes in parallel—let the network choose.
Inception Module:
Input
  ├─ 1×1 conv
  ├─ 1×1 conv → 3×3 conv
  ├─ 1×1 conv → 5×5 conv  
  └─ 3×3 MaxPool → 1×1 conv
      ↓
  Concatenate along channel dimension
1×1 Convolution Role:

Dimensionality reduction (cheaper than 3×3, 5×5 directly)
Cross-channel mixing
Additional non-linearity

Example: To compute 5×5 conv with 256 input and output channels:

Direct: \(5 \times 5 \times 256 \times 256 = 1{,}638{,}400\) params
With 1×1 bottleneck (256→64→256): \(1 \times 1 \times 256 \times 64 + 5 \times 5 \times 64 \times 256 = 425{,}984\) params

Trade-off: More architectural complexity vs. parameter efficiency and multi-scale features.






Figure 3.6: Inception architecture overview. Image Source: (Ng 2015).

title: 3  Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
3.7 CNNs: Design Principles
Principle 1: Depth Over Width

50-layer ResNet outperforms 10-layer wider network
Hierarchical feature learning requires depth

Principle 2: Small Filters (3×3)

Stack of 3×3 > single large filter
More non-linearity, fewer parameters
VGG, ResNet, modern architectures use 3×3 almost exclusively

Principle 3: Skip Connections for Depth

Essential for networks >30 layers
DenseNet: connect ALL previous layers

Principle 4: Bottlenecks for Efficiency

1×1 conv reduces channels before expensive 3×3/5×5
Inception, ResNet-50+, MobileNet all use this

Principle 5: Reduce Spatial Dimensions Gradually

Early aggressive pooling loses information
Modern: stride-2 convs at specific points (ResNet stages)

Principle 6: Increase Channels as Resolution Decreases

Compensate for spatial reduction with more features
Pattern: 64 → 128 → 256 → 512 → 1024 channels

Interview Question: “Design a CNN for 512×512 images with limited compute.”
Answer Framework:

Early aggressive downsampling (7×7 stride-2, then 3×3 stride-2) → 128×128
Depthwise separable convs (MobileNet-style)
Fewer stages (3 instead of 5)
Bottleneck blocks with small expansion factor
Global average pooling (no FC layers)

title: 4  Detection and Segmentation
text:
4.1 Object Detection
Task Definition: Given image \(\mathbf{I}\), output set of bounding boxes \(\{(x, y, w, h, c, p)\}\) where: - \((x,y)\) = box center - \((w,h)\) = width, height - \(c \in \{1, \ldots, C\}\) = object class - \(p \in [0,1]\) = confidence score
Challenges: 1. Multiple objects: Variable number per image 2. Scale variation: Objects from 10×10 to 500×500 pixels 3. Occlusion: Partially hidden objects 4. Dense overlapping predictions: Must suppress duplicates
Paradigms: - Two-Stage (R-CNN family): Propose regions → classify/refine - Single-Stage (YOLO, SSD): Directly predict boxes at multiple scales

title: 4  Detection and Segmentation
text:
4.1.1 Two-Stage Detectors: Faster R-CNN
Architecture Overview:
Image → CNN Backbone → Feature Maps 
                         ↓
                    [Stage 1: RPN]
                         ↓
                Region Proposals (~2000)
                         ↓
                    [ROI Pooling]
                         ↓
                   [Stage 2: R-CNN]
                         ↓
                (Class, Box Refinement)

4.1.1.1 Region Proposal Network (RPN)
Purpose: Generate ~2000 candidate object locations (proposals).
Mechanism: 1. Slide 3×3 conv over feature map 2. At each location, predict \(k\) anchor boxes (different scales/ratios) - Scales: {128², 256², 512²} - Ratios: {1:1, 1:2, 2:1} - Total: \(k = 9\) anchors per location

For each anchor, predict:

Objectness: \(p_{\text{obj}} \in [0,1]\) (object vs. background)
Box offsets: \((t_x, t_y, t_w, t_h)\) to refine anchor


Anchor Box Parametrization: Given anchor \((x_a, y_a, w_a, h_a)\), predicted box: \[x = x_a + w_a \cdot t_x, \quad y = y_a + h_a \cdot t_y\] \[w = w_a \cdot \exp(t_w), \quad h = h_a \cdot \exp(t_h)\]
Loss Function: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{RPN}} = \frac{1}{N_{\text{cls}}} \sum_i \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(p_i, p_i^*) + \lambda \frac{1}{N_{\text{reg}}} \sum_i p_i^* \mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}(\mathbf{t}_i, \mathbf{t}_i^*)\]
where: - \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}\) = binary cross-entropy (object vs. not) - \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}\) = smooth L1 loss: \(\text{smooth}_{L1}(x) = \begin{cases} 0.5x^2 & |x| < 1 \\ |x| - 0.5 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\) - \(p_i^* \in \{0,1\}\) = ground truth objectness - Regression loss only for positive anchors (\(p_i^* = 1\))
Label Assignment: - Positive: IoU > 0.7 with any ground truth, or highest IoU for a GT - Negative: IoU < 0.3 with all ground truths - Ignore: 0.3 ≤ IoU ≤ 0.7 (don’t contribute to loss)
Training Details: - Sample 256 anchors per image (128 positive, 128 negative) - Positive samples often scarce → pad with negatives - Cross-boundary anchors ignored during training



4.1.1.2 ROI Pooling
Purpose: Extract fixed-size features from variable-size proposals.
Algorithm: 1. Project proposal onto feature map (divide coords by network stride) 2. Divide region into \(H \times W\) grid (e.g., 7×7) 3. Max-pool within each grid cell
Example: - Proposal: 145×200 pixels at input - Feature map stride: 16 → proposal is 9.06×12.5 feature map cells - ROI Pooling: divide into 7×7 → each cell ~1.3×1.8 features → max-pool
Problem - Misalignment: Quantization (rounding coords) causes misalignment, hurting segmentation.
Solution - ROI Align (Mask R-CNN): - Use bilinear interpolation instead of rounding - Sample 4 points per grid cell, interpolate, then max-pool - Result: Better localization for masks



4.1.1.3 R-CNN Head (Stage 2)
Input: Fixed 7×7×512 features from ROI Pooling
Architecture:
ROI Features → FC(4096) → ReLU → Dropout
             → FC(4096) → ReLU → Dropout
             → Split:
                 ├─ Classification: FC(C+1)  [C classes + background]
                 └─ Box Regression: FC(4×C)  [per-class box refinement]
Loss Function: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(c, c^*) + \lambda [c^* > 0] \mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}(\mathbf{t}^{c^*}, \mathbf{t}^{c^*}_{\text{gt}})\]

Classification: multi-class cross-entropy
Regression: smooth L1, only for non-background classes
\(c^* = 0\) is background → no box loss

Training Strategy (4-Step Alternating): 1. Train RPN alone 2. Train R-CNN with frozen RPN proposals 3. Fine-tune RPN with R-CNN backbone frozen 4. Fine-tune R-CNN head
Modern implementations use approximate joint training (single-stage, more stable).

Faster R-CNN Summary: - Pros: High accuracy, flexible (any CNN backbone), strong for small objects - Cons: Slow (two-stage), complex training, many hyperparameters - Use When: Accuracy is critical (autonomous vehicles, medical imaging) - Avoid When: Real-time constraint (use YOLO instead)




4.1.2 2.2.2 Single-Stage Detectors: YOLO
Philosophy: “You Only Look Once”—predict all boxes in one forward pass.
YOLO Architecture (YOLOv3 as example):
Image → DarkNet-53 Backbone 
       → Feature Pyramid (3 scales)
       → Dense Predictions
Grid-Based Prediction: 1. Divide image into \(S \times S\) grid (e.g., 13×13) 2. Each grid cell predicts \(B\) bounding boxes (e.g., \(B=3\)) 3. For each box, predict: - Box coordinates: \((t_x, t_y, t_w, t_h)\) - Objectness: \(p_{\text{obj}}\) - Class probabilities: \((p_1, \ldots, p_C)\)
Total predictions: \(S \times S \times B \times (5 + C)\) values
For \(S=13\), \(B=3\), \(C=80\) (COCO): \(13 \times 13 \times 3 \times 85 = 43{,}095\) predictions
Box Decoding (relative to grid cell): \[b_x = \sigma(t_x) + c_x, \quad b_y = \sigma(t_y) + c_y\] \[b_w = p_w \cdot e^{t_w}, \quad b_h = p_h \cdot e^{t_h}\]
where \((c_x, c_y)\) = grid cell offset, \((p_w, p_h)\) = anchor dimensions.
Loss Function (YOLOv3): \[\mathcal{L} = \lambda_{\text{coord}} \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{1}_{ij}^{\text{obj}} \left[(t_x - \hat{t}_x)^2 + (t_y - \hat{t}_y)^2 + (t_w - \hat{t}_w)^2 + (t_h - \hat{t}_h)^2\right]\] \[+ \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{1}_{ij}^{\text{obj}} \text{BCE}(C_{ij}, \hat{C}_{ij})\] \[+ \lambda_{\text{noobj}} \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{1}_{ij}^{\text{noobj}} \text{BCE}(C_{ij}, \hat{C}_{ij})\] \[+ \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{1}_{ij}^{\text{obj}} \sum_{c \in \text{classes}} \text{BCE}(p_{ij}(c), \hat{p}_{ij}(c))\]
where: - \(\mathbb{1}_{ij}^{\text{obj}} = 1\) if box \(j\) in cell \(i\) is responsible for object - \(\lambda_{\text{coord}} = 5\), \(\lambda_{\text{noobj}} = 0.5\) (balance localization vs. classification) - BCE = binary cross-entropy
Key Insight: - Coordinate loss: Only when cell contains object - No-object loss: Down-weighted (most cells are background) - Class loss: Only for cells with objects
Multi-Scale Predictions (YOLOv3+): - Predict at 3 scales: 13×13, 26×26, 52×52 - Small objects → fine grid (52×52) - Large objects → coarse grid (13×13) - Uses Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) structure
YOLO Advantages: - Speed: 30-60 FPS (real-time) - Global context: Sees entire image (vs. RPN local proposals) - Fewer false positives on background
YOLO Disadvantages: - Small objects: Struggles when multiple objects in same grid cell - Unusual aspect ratios: Fixed anchor boxes may not fit well - Localization: Less precise than two-stage detectors
Interview Insight: “YOLO vs. Faster R-CNN?” Answer framework: - Speed: YOLO 10× faster (single-stage) - Accuracy: Faster R-CNN slight edge on COCO mAP - Small objects: Faster R-CNN better (RPN + multi-scale RoIs) - Deployment: YOLO for real-time, Faster R-CNN when accuracy critical



4.1.3 2.2.3 Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)
Problem: Detectors generate many overlapping boxes for same object.
Algorithm:
def nms(boxes, scores, iou_threshold=0.5):
    """
    boxes: (N, 4) - [x1, y1, x2, y2]
    scores: (N,) - confidence scores
    """
    # Sort by score descending
    order = scores.argsort()[::-1]
    keep = []
    
    while len(order) > 0:
        i = order[0]
        keep.append(i)
        
        # Compute IoU with remaining boxes
        ious = compute_iou(boxes[i], boxes[order[1:]])
        
        # Keep only boxes with IoU < threshold
        order = order[1:][ious < iou_threshold]
    
    return keep

def compute_iou(box1, box2):
    """IoU between two boxes"""
    x1 = max(box1[0], box2[0])
    y1 = max(box1[1], box2[1])
    x2 = min(box1[2], box2[2])
    y2 = min(box1[3], box2[3])
    
    intersection = max(0, x2 - x1) * max(0, y2 - y1)
    area1 = (box1[2] - box1[0]) * (box1[3] - box1[1])
    area2 = (box2[2] - box2[0]) * (box2[3] - box2[1])
    union = area1 + area2 - intersection
    
    return intersection / union
Complexity: \(O(N^2)\) IoU computations (can be optimized with spatial hashing)
Threshold Selection: - Low (0.3-0.4): Aggressive suppression → fewer duplicates, may miss nearby objects - High (0.6-0.7): Keep more boxes → more duplicates, better recall
Per-Class NMS: In multi-class detection, run NMS separately per class (car boxes don’t suppress person boxes).
Soft-NMS (Bodla et al., 2017): Instead of hard removal, decay scores based on IoU: \[s_i = \begin{cases} s_i & \text{IoU}(\mathcal{M}, b_i) < N_t \\ s_i \cdot e^{-\frac{\text{IoU}(\mathcal{M}, b_i)^2}{\sigma}} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
where \(\mathcal{M}\) is the current maximum box.
Result: Boxes with high IoU get down-weighted instead of removed → better recall.

title: 4  Detection and Segmentation
text:
4.2 2.3 Semantic Segmentation
Task: Assign class label to every pixel: \(f: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \rightarrow \{1, \ldots, C\}^{H \times W}\)
Challenges: - Resolution: Need pixel-level predictions (vs. classification’s single label) - Context: Local and global information both matter - Efficiency: Dense predictions over full image


4.2.1 2.3.1 U-Net (2015)
Architecture Philosophy: Encoder-decoder with skip connections.
Encoder (Contracting Path):
Input (572×572)
→ Conv-ReLU-Conv-ReLU → Skip1 (570×570, 64 ch)
→ MaxPool
→ Conv-ReLU-Conv-ReLU → Skip2 (280×280, 128 ch)
→ MaxPool
...
→ Bottleneck (28×28, 1024 ch)
Decoder (Expansive Path):
Bottleneck
→ UpConv → Concat(Skip4) → Conv-ReLU-Conv-ReLU
→ UpConv → Concat(Skip3) → Conv-ReLU-Conv-ReLU
...
→ Conv 1×1 → Output (388×388, C classes)
Key Innovation - Skip Connections: - Encoder captures what (semantic information) - Decoder recovers where (spatial details) - Skip connections provide high-res features to decoder
Why This Works: - Early layers: fine details (edges, textures) - Deep layers: semantic meaning (object identity) - Combining both: precise boundaries + correct labels
Loss: Pixel-wise softmax cross-entropy \[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{H \cdot W} \sum_{i,j} \sum_{c=1}^C y_{ij}^{(c)} \log \hat{y}_{ij}^{(c)}\]
U-Net Variants: - 3D U-Net: For volumetric data (medical CT/MRI) - U-Net++: Nested skip connections - Attention U-Net: Attention gates in skip connections
Applications: Medical imaging (won ISBI challenge), satellite imagery, microscopy



4.2.2 2.3.2 DeepLab v3+ (2018)
Core Ideas: 1. Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP): Multi-scale context 2. Encoder-Decoder: U-Net-like structure 3. Depthwise Separable Convs: Efficiency
ASPP Module:
Feature Map
  ├─ 1×1 conv
  ├─ 3×3 atrous conv, rate=6
  ├─ 3×3 atrous conv, rate=12
  ├─ 3×3 atrous conv, rate=18
  └─ Global Average Pool → 1×1 conv → Upsample
      ↓
  Concatenate → 1×1 conv → Output
Why Multiple Dilation Rates? - rate=6: captures medium context (~13×13 effective) - rate=12: large context (~25×25 effective) - rate=18: very large context (~37×37 effective) - Global pooling: image-level features
Motivation: Objects vary in scale—need multi-scale receptive fields.
Loss Function: - Pixel-wise cross-entropy (standard) - Focal Loss (optional, for class imbalance): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{focal}} = -\alpha (1 - \hat{y})^\gamma \log \hat{y}\]
where \(\gamma=2\) down-weights easy examples (high \(\hat{y}\)), focuses on hard pixels.
DeepLab Performance: - PASCAL VOC 2012: 89.0% mIoU - Cityscapes: 82.1% mIoU - Real-time variants exist (MobileNet backbone)



4.2.3 2.3.3 Mask R-CNN (2017)
Extension: Faster R-CNN + instance segmentation head.
Architecture:
Image → ResNet-FPN
       → RPN → ROI Align
       → Parallel Heads:
           ├─ Box Classification (C+1 classes)
           ├─ Box Regression (4 coords)
           └─ Mask Prediction (C × 28×28 binary masks)
Mask Head: - Input: 14×14 ROI features from ROI Align - Architecture: 4× Conv(256, 3×3) → Deconv(256, 2×2) → Conv(C, 1×1) - Output: \(C\) binary masks of size 28×28 (one per class)
Loss Function: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{box}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{mask}}\]
where: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{mask}} = -\frac{1}{m^2} \sum_{i,j} [y_{ij} \log \hat{y}_{ij} + (1-y_{ij}) \log(1-\hat{y}_{ij})]\]
Key Detail: Loss computed only on ground-truth class mask (not all \(C\) masks).
ROI Align (vs. ROI Pooling): - ROI Pooling: Quantizes coordinates → misalignment - ROI Align: Bilinear interpolation at sub-pixel locations → precise
Example: - Proposal maps to feature map region [5.7, 8.3, 12.1, 15.9] - ROI Pooling rounds to [6, 8, 12, 16] → 0.3-0.9 pixel errors - ROI Align samples at exact 5.7, 8.3, etc. using interpolation
Impact: Critical for mask accuracy (2-3% mIoU improvement).
Mask R-CNN Applications: - Instance segmentation (COCO, LVIS datasets) - Keypoint detection (pose estimation) - Panoptic segmentation (with Stuff head)
Interview Question: “Mask R-CNN vs. U-Net?” Answer: - U-Net: Semantic (no instances), faster, simpler - Mask R-CNN: Instance-aware, slower (two-stage), handles occlusion better - Use U-Net for medical imaging, Mask R-CNN for autonomous driving



4.2.4 Interview Preparation Tips

Architectural depth: Know parameter counts, FLOPs for common models
Training dynamics: Batch size effects, learning rate schedules, convergence
Trade-offs: Accuracy vs. speed, memory vs. compute, model size vs. performance



4.2.5 Common Interview Questions

“YOLO vs. Faster R-CNN—when to use each?”

YOLO: real-time, simpler; Faster R-CNN: higher accuracy, better for small objects

title: 5  Vision Transformers
text:
5.2 Vision Transformer (ViT, 2020)
Core Idea: Apply standard Transformer directly to images by treating them as sequences of patches.

5.2.1 Architecture Overview
Step 1: Patch Embeddings
Split image into non-overlapping patches and project to embedding space:

Partition: Image \(\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}\) → patches \(\mathbf{x}_p \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times P \times 3}\)

Number of patches: \(N = \frac{H \cdot W}{P^2}\)
Example: 224×224 image, 16×16 patches → \(N = 196\) patches

Flatten: Each patch \(\mathbf{x}_p \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times P \times 3}\) → \(\mathbf{x}_p \in \mathbb{R}^{P^2 \cdot 3}\)
Linear Projection: Map to embedding dimension \(D\) \[\mathbf{z}_i^{(0)} = \mathbf{E} \cdot \text{Flatten}(\mathbf{x}_{p_i}), \quad \mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times (P^2 \cdot 3)}\]
Prepend Class Token: Add learnable \([\text{CLS}]\) token \[\mathbf{z}_0^{(0)} = \mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}}\]
Add Position Embeddings: Learnable 1D positional encodings \[\mathbf{z}^{(0)} = [\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}}; \mathbf{z}_1^{(0)}; \ldots; \mathbf{z}_N^{(0)}] + \mathbf{E}_{\text{pos}}\] where \(\mathbf{E}_{\text{pos}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1) \times D}\)

Result: Sequence of \(N+1\) tokens, each \(D\)-dimensional.

Step 2: Transformer Encoder
Stack \(L\) blocks, composed by a Multi-Head Self-Attention layer (MSA) and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MPA):
z'= MSA(LayerNorm(z)) + z
z = MLP(LayerNorm(z')) + z'
MSA layer (Multi-Head Self-Attention layer):
For each head \(h\): \[\mathbf{Q}_h = \mathbf{z} \mathbf{W}_h^Q, \quad \mathbf{K}_h = \mathbf{z} \mathbf{W}_h^K, \quad \mathbf{V}_h = \mathbf{z} \mathbf{W}_h^V\]
\[\text{head}_h = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}_h \mathbf{K}_h^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right) \mathbf{V}_h\] \[(  d = D/H \text{ is the dimension per head} )\]
Concatenate and project: \[\text{MSA}(\mathbf{z}) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_H) \mathbf{W}^O\]
MLP Block: \[\text{MLP}(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{W}_2 \cdot \text{GELU}(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{z} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2\]
\[\big(\text{typically a 4× expansion } \mathbf{W}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times 4D}, \mathbf{W}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{4D \times D} \big)\]

3. Classification: MLP head on \([\text{CLS}]\) token → class logits
\[y = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{head}} \cdot \mathbf{z}_0^{(L)} + \mathbf{b}_{\text{head}})\]
Why \([\text{CLS}]\) token?

Aggregates global information through self-attention
Similar to BERT’s \([\text{CLS}]\) for sentence classification
Alternative: Global average pooling over all patch embeddings

5.2.3 Computational Complexity
Self-Attention: \(O(N^2 \cdot D)\) per layer, where \(N = (H/P)^2\) patches.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class PatchEmbed(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, img_size=224, patch_size=16, in_chans=3, embed_dim=768):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_patches = (img_size // patch_size) ** 2
        # Conv2d with kernel=stride=patch_size acts as patching + projection
        self.proj = nn.Conv2d(in_chans, embed_dim, 
                             kernel_size=patch_size, stride=patch_size)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (B, 3, H, W)
        x = self.proj(x)  # (B, embed_dim, H/P, W/P)
        x = x.flatten(2)  # (B, embed_dim, num_patches)
        x = x.transpose(1, 2)  # (B, num_patches, embed_dim)
        return x

class VisionTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, img_size=224, patch_size=16, num_classes=1000,
                 embed_dim=768, depth=12, num_heads=12, mlp_ratio=4.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.patch_embed = PatchEmbed(img_size, patch_size, 3, embed_dim)
        num_patches = self.patch_embed.num_patches
        
        # Learnable parameters
        self.cls_token = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, embed_dim))
        self.pos_embed = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, num_patches + 1, embed_dim))
        
        # Transformer encoder
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([
            TransformerBlock(embed_dim, num_heads, mlp_ratio)
            for _ in range(depth)
        ])
        
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(embed_dim)
        self.head = nn.Linear(embed_dim, num_classes)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        B = x.shape[0]
        x = self.patch_embed(x)  # (B, N, D)
        
        # Prepend CLS token
        cls_tokens = self.cls_token.expand(B, -1, -1)
        x = torch.cat([cls_tokens, x], dim=1)  # (B, N+1, D)
        
        # Add position embeddings
        x = x + self.pos_embed
        
        # Apply transformer blocks
        for block in self.blocks:
            x = block(x)
        
        x = self.norm(x)
        
        # Classification head on CLS token
        return self.head(x[:, 0])

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, num_heads, mlp_ratio=4.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(dim)
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(dim, num_heads, batch_first=True)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(dim)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(dim, int(dim * mlp_ratio)),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(int(dim * mlp_ratio), dim)
        )
    
    def forward(self, x):
        # Self-attention with residual
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x), self.norm1(x), self.norm1(x))[0]
        # MLP with residual
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        return x
Key Implementation Details:

Using Conv2d for patching is more efficient than reshaping
batch_first=True in PyTorch’s MultiheadAttention
Pre-LayerNorm (norm before attention) is more stable than post-norm


Interview Insights:
Q: “Why does ViT need so much data?” A: CNNs have built-in inductive biases (locality, translation equivariance). ViT has none—must learn spatial relationships from data. With enough data, this flexibility becomes an advantage (learns task-specific patterns).
Q: “When to use ViT over CNN?” A: - Use ViT: Large pre-trained models available, downstream task has sufficient data, need for global context (medical imaging, satellite) - Use CNN: Limited data, real-time inference (lower FLOPs), well-understood architectures
Q: “How to make ViT more efficient?” A:

Hierarchical architectures (Swin)
Linear attention approximations
Smaller patch sizes initially (higher resolution early, then merge)
Hybrid CNN-Transformer (CNN stem + Transformer)

5.3 DeiT: Data-Efficient Training (2021)
Problem: ViT requires very large training datasets s.a. ImageNet-21K (14M images) or JFT (300M).
Solution: Knowledge distillation enables training on ImageNet-1K only.
Architecture:
Add distillation token \(\mathbf{z}_{\text{dist}}\) alongside \([\text{CLS}]\) to a total of \(N+2\) tokens:
\[\mathbf{z}^{(0)} = [\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}}; \mathbf{z}_{\text{dist}}; \mathbf{z}_1^{(0)}; \ldots; \mathbf{z}_N^{(0)}] + \mathbf{E}_{\text{pos}}\]
Consider two classification heads:

\(\mathbf{y}_{\text{cls}} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{cls}} \mathbf{z}_0^{(L)})\) — standard prediction
\(\mathbf{y}_{\text{dist}} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{dist}} \mathbf{z}_1^{(L)})\) — distillation prediction

Loss: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(y, \hat{y}_{\text{cls}}) + \alpha \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(y, \hat{y}_{\text{dist}}) + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}}(y_{\text{teacher}}, \hat{y}_{\text{dist}})\]
where \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} = \text{KL}\left(\text{softmax}(y_{\text{teacher}}/T) \|
\text{softmax}(y_{\text{dist}}/T)\right)\) is the Knowledge Distillation Loss (Hinton et al., 2015), with \(T\) the temperature parameter, typically \(T=3\) for softer distributions.
Key Findings:

CNN teacher (RegNetY-16GF) works better than Transformer teacher
Achieves 81.8% on ImageNet-1K without external pre-training
Inference: Can use \((\hat{y}_{\text{cls}} + \hat{y}_{\text{dist}})/2\) for best performance

Impact: Democratized ViT training—no need for web-scale datasets.

title: 5  Vision Transformers
text:
5.4 Swin Transformer (2021)
Motivation: ViT’s \(O(N^2)\) complexity doesn’t scale to:

High-resolution images (detection, segmentation need 800×800+)
Dense prediction tasks (every pixel needs attention)

Solution: Hierarchical architecture with local windowed attention + shifted windows for global receptive field.


5.4.1 Key Mechanisms
1. Window Attention (W-MSA):

Partition into \(M \times M\) non-overlapping windows (typically \(M=7\))
Self-attention within each window only
Complexity: \(O(hw \cdot M^2)\) — linear in image size

2. Shifted Window Attention (SW-MSA):

Alternate between regular and shifted (\(M/2\) offset) window partitions
Enables cross-window communication
Implemented efficiently via cyclic shift + masking

3. Patch Merging (like CNN pooling):

Concatenate 2×2 neighbors (4C channels)
Linear projection: \(4C → 2C\)
Result: \(4×\) fewer tokens, \(2×\) channels

Architecture (4 Stages - analogous to CNN feature pyramid):
Input (224×224×3)
  ↓ Patch Partition (4×4) → (56×56, 96 channels)
  ↓ Stage 1: 2× Swin Blocks (56×56, 96 ch)
  ↓ Patch Merging → (28×28, 192 ch)
  ↓ Stage 2: 2× Swin Blocks (28×28, 192 ch)
  ↓ Patch Merging → (14×14, 384 ch)
  ↓ Stage 3: 6× Swin Blocks (14×14, 384 ch)
  ↓ Patch Merging → (7×7, 768 ch)
  ↓ Stage 4: 2× Swin Blocks (7×7, 768 ch)
  ↓ Classification Head
Key Properties:

Spatial resolution decreases (like CNN pooling)
Channel count increases (compensation)
Produces multi-scale features (compatible with FPN for detection)

Interview Insights:
Q: “Swin vs. ViT trade-offs?”
A:

Swin: Efficient (\(O(N)\)), hierarchical features, better for dense tasks

ViT: Simpler, global attention from layer 1, better for large-scale pre-training

Q: “Why shifted windows instead of overlapping windows?”
A: Overlapping windows would increase computation (more tokens per window). Shifting provides cross-window communication with zero overhead via cyclic shift trick.
Q: “Can Swin replace CNNs entirely?”
A: In many cases, yes—especially for detection/segmentation. CNNs still win for:

Very small datasets (better inductive bias)

Real-time inference (lower latency)

Hardware without optimized attention kernels
