class SwinTransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, num_heads, window_size=7, shift_size=0):
        super().__init__()
        self.window_size = window_size
        self.shift_size = shift_size
        
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(dim)
        self.attn = WindowAttention(dim, window_size, num_heads)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(dim)
        self.mlp = MLP(dim, int(dim * 4))
    
    def forward(self, x):
        H, W = self.H, self.W
        B, L, C = x.shape
        
        shortcut = x
        x = self.norm1(x)
        x = x.view(B, H, W, C)
        
        # Cyclic shift if needed
        if self.shift_size > 0:
            shifted_x = torch.roll(x, shifts=(-self.shift_size, -self.shift_size), 
                                   dims=(1, 2))
        else:
            shifted_x = x
        
        # Partition windows
        x_windows = window_partition(shifted_x, self.window_size)
        
        # W-MSA or SW-MSA
        attn_windows = self.attn(x_windows)
        
        # Merge windows
        shifted_x = window_reverse(attn_windows, self.window_size, H, W)
        
        # Reverse cyclic shift
        if self.shift_size > 0:
            x = torch.roll(shifted_x, shifts=(self.shift_size, self.shift_size), 
                          dims=(1, 2))
        else:
            x = shifted_x
        
        x = x.view(B, H * W, C)
        
        # Residual connection
        x = shortcut + x
        
        # MLP with residual
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        
        return x

5.5 DETR: Detection Transformer (2020)
Paradigm: Treat object detection as direct set prediction (no anchors, no NMS).
Key Components:

Backbone: Standard ResNet-50 (could be any CNN)
Encoder: Processes image features with self-attention
Decoder: 100 learnable object queries attend to encoder output
Prediction Head: Each query predicts (class, box) or “no object”

Architecture:
Image → CNN Backbone → Flatten + Positional Encoding
      → Transformer Encoder (6 layers)
      → Transformer Decoder (6 layers, 100 object queries)
      → Prediction Heads → {class, bbox} × 100
Object Queries:

100 learnable embeddings \(\mathbf{q}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{100} \in \mathbb{R}^D\) initialized randomly.
Each of these queries can “search” for an object via cross-attention to encoder features.
COCO images have \(<100\) objects on average. Excess queries predict “no object” class


5.5.1 Training with Bipartite Matching
Ground truth has variable number of objects (1-100), predictions are fixed (100).
Hungarian Algorithm finds optimal one-to-one matching between predictions and ground truth: \[\sigma^* = \arg\min_{\sigma} \sum_{j} \left[-\hat{p}_{c_j}(\sigma(j)) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}(\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{\sigma(j)}, \mathbf{b}_j)\right]\]
Loss: \[\mathcal{L} = \sum_{j} \left[-\log \hat{p}_{c_j}(\sigma^*(j)) + \lambda_{\text{L1}}\|\hat{\mathbf{b}} - \mathbf{b}\|_1 + \lambda_{\text{GIoU}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{GIoU}}\right]\]
Key Innovation: Set prediction with matching → NMS unnecessary (each object predicted once).
This is more elegant than setting a IoU threshold for NMS, a hand-crafted heuristic.

5.6 Deformable DETR (2021)
Problem: DETR is slow (500 epochs) and struggles with small objects.
Solution - Deformable Attention:

Attend to only \(K=4\) learned reference points (vs. all \(N\) pixels)
Multi-scale sampling from feature pyramid

Standard Attention (query \(\mathbf{q}\), keys \(\{\mathbf{k}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{k}_N\}\)): \[\text{Attn}(\mathbf{q}, \{\mathbf{k}_i\}_{i=1}^N) = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i \mathbf{v}_i\]
where \(\alpha_i = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}_i}{\sqrt{d}}\right)\).
Deformable Attention:
\[\text{DeformAttn}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}_{\text{ref}}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{i} \cdot \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref}} + \Delta \mathbf{p}_{mk})\]
where \(\Delta \mathbf{p}_{k}\) are learned offsets. where:

\(\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref}} \in \mathbb{R}^2\) = reference point (e.g., query’s current best guess)
\(\Delta \mathbf{p}_{k} \in \mathbb{R}^2\) = learned offset for sampling point \(k\)
\(\mathbf{x}(\mathbf{p})\) = feature at location \(\mathbf{p}\) (bilinear interpolation if non-integer)
\(\alpha_{k}\) = attention weight (learned)

Multi-Scale: Sample from multiple FPN levels → better small object detection.
\[\text{MSDeformAttn}(\mathbf{q}, \{\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref}}^l\}_{l=1}^L, \{\mathbf{x}^l\}_{l=1}^L) =
\mathbf{W}_m \sum_{l=1}^L \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{mlk} \cdot \mathbf{x}^l(\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref}}^l + \Delta \mathbf{p}_{mlk})\]

Small objects → sample from high-res features
Large objects → sample from low-res features
Query learns which scales are relevant

Complexity: DETR: \(O(N_q \cdot N_k \cdot D)\) → quadratic.
Deformable DETR: \(O(N_q \cdot K \cdot D)\), where \(K\) is constant → linear

Q: “Why does deformable attention help small objects?” A: Standard attention diffuses over large feature maps. Deformable attention focuses on a small learned set of relevant locations → sharper attention on small objects. Multi-scale sampling also helps by using high-resolution features.
Q: “Can deformable attention replace standard attention everywhere?” A: Not always. Deformable attention assumes spatial structure (2D images). Standard attention is more general (works for any sequence). For vision at scale, deformable is often better.
Q: “How to implement bilinear sampling for non-integer coordinates?” A: PyTorch’s F.grid_sample with mode='bilinear'. Used in Spatial Transformer Networks (2015) and Deformable Convolutions (2017).

5.7 Segment Anything Model (SAM, 2023)
Vision: Foundation model for segmentation—segment any object from any prompt, zero-shot.
Inspiration from NLP: GPT-3 for language → SAM for segmentation.

Masks → small CNN (4 conv layers)

Bipartite matching ensures one-to-one assignment → no duplicate predictions

text:
6.1 Motivation and Paradigm Overview
The Labeling Bottleneck: Training large vision models requires massive datasets, but manual annotation is expensive and slow. ImageNet took 3 years and $50K to label 14M images. Modern foundation models need billions of images.
Self-Supervised Learning (SSL): Learn useful visual representations from unlabeled data by creating pretext tasks where supervision comes from the data itself.
Why SSL Works: Natural images have rich structure—spatial coherence, semantic consistency across augmentations, predictable patterns. SSL exploits these properties to learn features transferable to downstream tasks.
Performance Evolution: - 2018: SSL lags supervised by 10%+ on ImageNet - 2020: SSL matches supervised (SimCLR, MoCo) - 2023: SSL outperforms supervised for transfer (DINOv2: 82.1% linear probe vs. 76.5% supervised)

title: 6  Self-Supervised Learning
text:
6.2 Taxonomy of Self-Supervised Approaches
Two Main Paradigms:

Invariance-Based Learning: Learn features invariant to augmentations \((f(x) \approx f(\text{Aug}(x))\).
The main challenge is how to prevent collapse to the constant representation.

Similarity-Based Methods

Contrastive Learning: Explicit negative samples (SimCLR, MoCo, PIRL)
Clustering: Discrete cluster assignments (DeepCluster, SwAV)
Self-Distillation: Asymmetry + momentum (BYOL, SimSiam, DINO)

Redundancy Reduction

Decorrelation Methods: Feature covariance → identity (Barlow Twins, VICReg)


Reconstructive Learning: Learn by predicting \(x\) from corrupted/masked input \(\tilde{x}\) (MAE, VideoMAE).
No collapse issue (reconstruction target is informative).
The main challenge is how to avoid low-level texture copying.

Organization of This Chapter: We first cover invariance-based methods (§6.3), subdivided by their collapse prevention mechanism, then reconstructive approaches (§6.4).

Invariance-Based Learning
Goal: Learn features invariant to augmentations \(f(x) \approx f(\text{Aug}(x))\).
Challenge: Avoiding Collapse. Given the objective of “making features of augmented views similar” the network could simply learn the Trivial Solution:
\[f_\theta(x) = c \quad \forall x\]

Collapse Types:

Complete collapse: All outputs identical
Dimensional collapse: All variance in few dimensions
Mode collapse: Different samples map to same points

title: 6  Self-Supervised Learning
text:
6.3 Similarity-Based Methods
Core Objective: Maximize similarity between augmented views of same image.
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{sim}} = d(f_\theta(\text{Aug}_1(x)), f_\theta(\text{Aug}_2(x)))\]
where \(d\) is distance metric (cosine, MSE). Methods differ in collapse prevention.


6.3.1 Contrastive Learning
Principle: Explicitly push apart different images (negatives) while pulling together augmented views (positives).
General Contrastive Loss: \[\mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp(\text{sim}(f(x^+), f(x))/\tau)}{\exp(\text{sim}(f(x^+), f(x))/\tau) + \sum_{x^- \in \mathcal{N}} \exp(\text{sim}(f(x^-), f(x))/\tau)}\]
where \(x^+\) is positive pair, \(\mathcal{N}\) is negative set, \(\tau=0.1\) is temperature.
Key Design Choice: How to obtain negative samples?

SimCLR (2020): In-Batch Negatives
Algorithm:

Sample mini-batch of \(N\) images
Apply two random augmentations to each → \(2N\) views
Encode: \(\mathbf{z}_i = g(f(t_i(x)))\) where \(g\) is projection MLP
For each view \(i\), compute loss against its positive pair \(j\) and \(2N-2\) negatives

InfoNCE Loss (Noise Contrastive Estimation) also called
NT-Xent Loss (Normalized Temperature-scaled Cross-Entropy): \[\mathcal{L}_i = -\log \frac{\exp(\text{sim}(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_j)/\tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{2N} \mathbb{1}_{k \neq i} \exp(\text{sim}(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_k)/\tau)}\] where \(\text{sim}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{v} / (\|\mathbf{u}\| \|\mathbf{v}\|)\) is cosine similarity, \(\tau = 0.1\) is temperature.
Critical Components:

Large batches (4096-8192): More negatives → better discrimination
Strong augmentations: Random crop, color jitter, Gaussian blur
Projection head: 2-layer MLP (128d output) improves features
Temperature: \(\tau=0.1\) sharpens distribution

Performance: ResNet-50, 69.3% ImageNet linear probe (200 epochs)
Limitation: Requires very large batches (memory-intensive on multi-GPU).

MoCo (2020) - Queue-Based Negatives:
Innovation: Decouple dictionary size from batch size using queue + momentum encoder.
Architecture Components:
Query Encoder f_q: Learnable (gradient descent)
Key Encoder f_k:   Momentum EMA of f_q  
Queue:             K=65,536 encoded keys
Algorithm:

Encode query: \(\mathbf{q} = f_q(\text{aug}_1(x))\) (with gradient)
Encode key: \(\mathbf{k} = f_k(\text{aug}_2(x))\) (no gradient)
Loss: \(\mathbf{q}\) vs. \(\mathbf{k}\) (positive) and all queue keys (negatives)
Update queue: Enqueue \(\mathbf{k}\), dequeue oldest
Update \(f_k\): \(\theta_k \leftarrow m \theta_k + (1-m) \theta_q\) , where \(m=0.999\)

Why Momentum? Queue contains keys from different training iterations. Momentum ensures slow encoder evolution → consistent dictionary.
Advantages:

Large dictionary (65K) with small batches (256)
Memory-efficient: Queue stores features, not images
Consistent negatives across training

Performance: ResNet-50, 71.1% ImageNet linear probe (MoCo v2, 200 epochs)

PIRL (2020): Memory Bank Negatives
Approach: Negative samples from memory bank storing features of all training images.
Key Difference from MoCo: - PIRL: Memory bank stores features of all dataset images - MoCo: Queue stores recent mini-batch features
NCE Loss (Noise Contrastive Estimation): \[\mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp(f(x)^\top f(t(x))/\tau)}{\exp(f(x)^\top f(t(x))/\tau) + \sum_{i=1}^K \exp(f(x)^\top f(x_i^-)/\tau)}\]
where \(K\) negatives sampled uniformly from memory bank.
Performance: Similar to MoCo v1 (~60% linear probe).

Key Insight - Contrastive Methods: Performance improves with:

More negatives (SimCLR: larger batches, MoCo: larger queues)
Consistent negatives (MoCo momentum encoder)
Stronger augmentations (color jitter + blur critical)




6.3.2 Clustering-Based Methods
Core Principle: Prevent collapse by assigning features to discrete clusters, then enforce consistency of cluster assignments across augmented views.
Advantage: No explicit negatives needed (cluster assignment provides discrimination).

DeepCluster (2018): Offline Clustering
Algorithm (alternating optimization) - Repeat each epoch:

Cluster Assignment: Run k-means on all image features \[c_i = \arg\min_k \|f(x_i) - \mu_k\|^2\]
Network Training: Train with cluster labels as pseudo-labels \[\mathcal{L} = -\sum_i \log p(c_i | x_i)\]

Analysis via Normalized Mutual Information:
To evaluate how meaningful the learned clusters are, DeepCluster compares its pseudo-labels \(A\) with the ground-truth ImageNet class labels \(B\) using Normalized Mutual Information: \[\text{NMI}(A, B) = \frac{2 \cdot I(A; B)}{H(A) + H(B)}\] where:
\(I(A;B)\) — mutual information: how much knowing the cluster assignment tells you about the true class.
\[I(A;B) = \sum_{a \in A} \sum_{b \in B} p(a,b) \log \frac{p(a,b)}{p(a)\,p(b)}\] \(H(A)\) and \(H(B)\) — entropies of the cluster and class label distributions. \[H(A) = -\sum_{a \in A} p(a)\log p(a), \quad H(B) = -\sum_{b \in B} p(b)\log p(b)\] Interpretation:

NMI = 1 → perfect alignment (clusters perfectly match classes)

NMI = 0 → no relation between clusters and classes

Findings:

Learned Clusters stabilize after ~50 epochs.
Learned Clusters roughly align with ImageNet classes (NMI ~0.4)
Best performance with k ≈ 10,000 clusters (10× more than ImageNet’s 1000 classes)

Limitation: k-means over full dataset is slow bottleneck (~1 hour/epoch).

SwAV (2020): - Swapped Assignment Prediction
Key Innovation: Online clustering** algorithm with Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization—no k-means needed.
Components:

Encoder: \(f_\theta\) (ResNet or ViT)
Prototype vectors: \(\mathbf{C} = [\mathbf{c}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{c}_K]\) (learnable, \(K\)=3000 typically)

Algorithm:

Extract features for two augmentations: \(\mathbf{z}_1 = f(\text{aug}_1(x))\), \(\mathbf{z}_2 = f(\text{aug}_2(x))\)
Compute soft cluster assignments (codes): \[\mathbf{q}_1 = \text{SinkhornKnopp}(\mathbf{z}_1^\top \mathbf{C} / \tau)\] where \(\mathbf{C} = [\mathbf{c}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{c}_K]\)
Swap Prediction: Predict \(\mathbf{q}_1\) from \(\mathbf{z}_2\) and vice versa

Sinkhorn-Knopp: Iterative normalization to make assignment matrix doubly stochastic

Row constraint: Each sample distributes across clusters (sum to 1)
Column constraint: Equal cluster usage (each cluster gets \(B/K\) samples)

Loss: Cross-entropy between predicted and target codes \[\mathcal{L} = \ell(\mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{q}_2) + \ell(\mathbf{z}_2, \mathbf{q}_1)\] \[\ell(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{q}) = -\sum_{k=1}^K q_k \log \frac{\exp(\mathbf{z}^\top \mathbf{c}_k / \tau)}{\sum_{k'} \exp(\mathbf{z}^\top \mathbf{c}_{k'} / \tau)}\]
Why Swapping? Predict cluster of one view from features of another → enforces consistency.
Multi-Crop Strategy:

2 global crops (224×224)
6 local crops (96×96)
Total 8 views per image → richer training signal

Key Advantages:

Online clustering (no k-means needed)
Works with small batches (256)
Faster than DeepCluster

Performance: ResNet-50, 71.8% ImageNet linear probe (200 epochs)



6.3.3 Self-Distillation Methods
Principle: Prevent collapse via asymmetry between two networks (no negatives needed).
General Framework:

Online network: Learnable encoder + predictor
Target network: Momentum encoder (no predictor)
Key: Asymmetry between the two architectures or between their gradient updates prevents collapse (such as stopping the gradient updates of target network)

Advantage: No negatives or clustering needed.

BYOL (2020) - Bootstrap Your Own Latent:
Architecture:
Online:  Encoder f_θ → Projection g_θ → Prediction h_θ
Target:  Encoder f_ξ → Projection g_ξ  (EMA, no predictor)
Algorithm:

Two augmentations: \(v, v' \sim \text{Aug}(x)\)
Online forward: \(\mathbf{q} = h_\theta(g_\theta(f_\theta(v)))\)
Target forward: \(\mathbf{z}' = \text{stop-gradient}(g_\xi(f_\xi(v')))\)
Loss (L2 on normalized features): \[\mathcal{L(v, v')} = \left\| \frac{\mathbf{q}}{\|\mathbf{q}\|_2} - \frac{\mathbf{z}'}{\|\mathbf{z}'\|_2} \right\|_2^2\]
Symmetrize: Also compute loss \(\mathcal{L}(v', v)\)
Update target: \(\theta' \leftarrow \tau \theta' + (1-\tau)\theta\),   where \(\tau=0.99\)

Why No Collapse?

Architecture Asymmetry: Predictor \(h\) only in online network
Stop-gradient: Target provides fixed targets (no gradient flow back)
Momentum: \(\tau = 0.99\) stabilizes target network

Intuition: Online network must predict target outputs, but target doesn’t “see” online predictions → information flow is one-way.
Performance: ResNet-50, 74.3% ImageNet linear probe (200 epochs)
Impact: Showed negative samples are not strictly necessary with right architecture.

SimSiam (2021) - Simplification:
Insight: Remove momentum encoder—just use stop-gradient!
Architecture:
Branch 1: Encoder f → Projection g → Prediction h
Branch 2: Encoder f → Projection g (shared, stop-gradient)
Loss (Negative cosine similarity, symmetrized over both views): \[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{h(g(f(x_1))) \cdot \text{stop-gradient}(g(f(x_2)))}{\|h(g(f(x_1)))\| \cdot \|\text{stop-gradient}(g(f(x_2)))\|}\]
Simpler than BYOL: - ✗ No momentum encoder (same \(f\) and \(g\) for both views) - ✓ Still has predictor \(h\) (critical for preventing collapse) - ✓ Still has Stop-gradient on one branch
Performance: ResNet-50, 71.3% ImageNet linear probe (200 epochs)
Advantage: Simplest SSL method — no negatives, no momentum, no clustering

DINO (2021) - Self-Distillation with ViT:
Innovation: Apply self-distillation to Vision Transformers with centering to prevent dimensional collapse.
Architecture:
Student: ViT (learned via gradient descent)
Teacher: ViT (EMA of student, τ=0.996)
Key Mechanisms:

Multi-crop: Teacher sees 2 global crops (224×224), student 2 global (224×224) + 8 local crops (96×96)
Centering: (prevent dimensional collapse — when one output dimension of the teacher consistently dominates, causing embeddings to lose diversity): A running mean (called the center) of the teacher’s outputs is maintained and subtracted each iteration: \[
c \leftarrow m \cdot c + (1 - m) \cdot \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B g_t(f_t(x_i))
\] where



$ c $: running mean of teacher outputs

$ m = 0.9 $: momentum for the update

$ B $: batch size

\(g_t(f_t(x_i))\): pre-softmax teacher output for image ( \(x_i\) ). The centered teacher probability distribution is then computed as:

\[
P_t = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{g_t(f_t(x)) - c}{\tau_t}\right)
\]

Temperature Sharpening:


Teacher: \(\tau_t = 0.04\) (sharp, confident pseudo-labels)
Student: \(\tau_s = 0.1\) (smooth, easier optimization)

Loss: Cross-entropy between teacher and student distributions \[\mathcal{L} = \sum_{i \in \text{crops}} H(P_t, P_s^{(i)})\]
where \(H(p, q) = -\sum_k p_k \log q_k\) is cross-entropy.
Emergent Properties:

Self-Attention Visualizations: Attention maps segment objects without segmentation labels!

ViT naturally learns to attend to object boundaries
Can extract object masks directly from attention

Strong k-NN performance: 75% ImageNet with frozen features

Performance:
ResNet-50, 75.3% ImageNet linear probe (300 epochs)
ViT-S/16,     77.0% ImageNet linear probe (300 epochs)






TipPseudocode





# Student forward (all 10 crops)
student_out = [student(crop) for crop in crops]  # 10 views
student_probs = [softmax(out / tau_s) for out in student_out]

# Teacher forward (2 global crops only)
with torch.no_grad():
    teacher_out = [teacher(global_crop) for global_crop in global_crops[:2]]
    teacher_out_centered = [out - center for out in teacher_out]
    teacher_probs = [softmax(out / tau_t) for out in teacher_out_centered]
    
    # Update center
    center = momentum * center + (1 - momentum) * teacher_out[0].mean(dim=0)

# Loss: each student view predicts each teacher view
loss = 0
for t_prob in teacher_probs:
    for s_prob in student_probs:
        loss += -torch.sum(t_prob * torch.log(s_prob), dim=-1).mean()




DINOv2 (2023) - Scaling Up:
Key Changes:

Data: 142M curated images (from 1B web images via retrieval + deduplication)
Training: iBOT (masked prediction) + DINO + regularizers (Sinkhorn-Knopp, KoLeo)
Scale: ViT-L/14, longer training

Result: 82.1% ImageNet linear probe (frozen features) — outperforms supervised pre-training.
Impact: General-purpose features usable out-of-the-box for segmentation, detection, depth estimation. SOTA across 20+ benchmarks.

DINOv3 (2025) - Gram Anchoring:
Problem: Long training (DINOv2 style) causes feature drift — dense features become “blurry” or inconsistent, hurting pixel-level tasks.
Solution: Preserve spatial feature correlations via Gram matrix loss,
matching second-order statistics (co-occurrence patterns of texture/style) rather than exact features.
Gram Matrix (from neural style transfer - Gatys et al., 2015): \[\mathbf{G}_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{HW} F_{ki} F_{kj}\]
where \(F \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times C}\) are spatial features (\(HW\) locations, \(C\) channels).
Gram Anchoring Loss: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Gram}} = \|\bar{\mathbf{G}}_s - \bar{\mathbf{G}}_t\|_F^2\]
where \(\bar{\mathbf{G}}\) is normalized Gram matrix: \[\bar{\mathbf{G}} = \frac{\mathbf{G}}{\|\mathbf{G}\|_F}\]
Why This Works:

Preserves second-order statistics (feature correlations)
Allows individual features to refine (first-order can change)
Maintains spatial consistency across training

Final Loss: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{Gram}}\)
Result: Stable dense features throughout long training, result in a large improvement on dense vision tasks such as segmentation and depth estimation:

Classification Result:   88.4% ImageNet linear probe (frozen features)
Detection Result:           66.1% COCO mAP (self-supervised, frozen features)
Segmentation Result: 63.0% ADE20K mIoU (self-supervised, frozen features)

title: 6  Self-Supervised Learning
text:
6.4 Redundancy Reduction Methods
Different Approach: Prevent collapse by decorrelating feature dimensions rather than using negatives or asymmetry.
Core Idea: Encourage cross-correlation matrix of features to be identity: \[\mathbf{C} \approx \mathbf{I}\]
where \(C_{ij} = \text{corr}(z_i, z_j)\) (correlation between feature dimensions \(i\) and \(j\) across batch).
Intuition:

Diagonal = 1: Features are invariant to augmentations (same image → same features)

Off-diagonal = 0: Features are non-redundant (different dimensions encode different information)


Barlow Twins (2021):
Loss Function: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{BT}} = \sum_i (1 - C_{ii})^2 + \lambda \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} C_{ij}^2\]
where:

First term:         Invariance to Augmentation (diagonal should be 1)
Second term:   Redundancy reduction (off-diagonal should be 0)
\(\lambda = 0.005\) balances the two terms

Cross-Correlation Matrix (computed over batch): \[C_{ij} = \frac{\sum_b z_{b,i}^A z_{b,j}^B}{\sqrt{\sum_b (z_{b,i}^A)^2} \sqrt{\sum_b (z_{b,j}^B)^2}}\]
where \(z_{b}^A, z_{b}^B\) are features from two augmentations, of an image \(b\) in the batch.
Properties:

Works with small batches (e.g. batch-size = 256) (unlike contrastive methods)
Highly dependent on augmentations (like contrastive methods)
Benefits from high-dimensional features (e.g. 8192d projection)

Performance: ResNet-50, 73.2% ImageNet linear probe (300 epochs)

VICReg (2021) - Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization:
More Explicit Formulation: Three separate loss terms.
\[\mathcal{L} = \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}} + \mu \mathcal{L}_{\text{var}} + \nu \mathcal{L}_{\text{cov}}\]
1. Invariance (MSE between views): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}} = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^d \|z_i^A - z_i^B\|^2\]
2. Variance (prevent collapse to constant): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{var}} = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^d \max(0, \gamma - \sqrt{\text{Var}(z_i) + \epsilon})\]
Encourages variance \(\geq \gamma\) (typically \(\gamma=1\)) for each dimension.
3. Covariance (decorrelate dimensions): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{cov}} = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i \neq j} \text{Cov}(z_i, z_j)^2\]
Typical Weights: \(\lambda=25\), \(\mu=25\), \(\nu=1\)
Advantage: More interpretable than Barlow Twins, similar performance.

Why Redundancy Reduction Works:

Decorrelation naturally prevents collapse (can’t collapse to one dimension if off-diagonals penalized)
No need for negatives, momentum, or asymmetry
Elegant mathematical formulation

title: 6  Self-Supervised Learning
text:
Reconstructive Learning
Different Paradigm: Instead of learning invariances, learn by predicting masked or corrupted input.
No Collapse Issue: Reconstruction target is informative (pixel values), prevents trivial solutions.
Challenge: Avoid low-level texture copying—want semantic features, not pixel-level memorization.

title: 6  Self-Supervised Learning
text:
6.5 Masked Auto-Encoding
MAE (2022) - Masked Auto-Encoding for Images:
Core Idea: Mask 75% of image patches, reconstruct from visible 25%.
Why 75% vs. BERT’s 15%?

Images more redundant than text (spatial continuity)
Low masking → local texture sufficient (too easy)
High masking → forces holistic understanding

Architecture:

Encoder (ViT):


Standard ViT transformer
Input: &nbsp ;  Only visible patches (25%) → 4× speedup
Output: Encoded visible features


Decoder (Small Transformer):


Smaller than encoder (8 layers vs. 24)
Input:     Encoded visible + mask tokens (learned embeddings)
Output: Reconstructed pixels for all patches

Loss: MSE on masked patches only \[\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|\text{Masked}|} \sum_{p \in \text{Masked}} \|\mathbf{x}_p - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_p\|^2\]
Key Design:

Asymmetric encoder-decoder (efficient)
Mask tokens added after encoder (encoder sees only 25%)
Minimal augmentation (just random crop)

Linear Probing
Protocol: Freeze pre-trained encoder, train linear classifier on top.
What it Measures:

Out-of-the-box usability: How useful are frozen features?

Supervised ResNet-50: 76.5%
MoCo v2 ResNet-50: 71.1%

title: 6  Self-Supervised Learning
text:
Dense Prediction Tasks
Plain ViTs output single-scale features, but dense tasks (detection, segmentation) require multi-scale feature pyramids.
Two frameworks are typically used to transfer the ViT features to dense tasks:
Feature Pyramid - ViT-Adapter (2023): - Augments ViT with lightweight conv + cross-attention adapters - Fuses intermediate ViT features into feature pyramid (FPN-like) - Provides scale-aware features for detecting small and large objects
Segmentation Head - Mask2Former (2022): Universal architecture with three components:

Backbone: SSL pre-trained ViT (frozen or fine-tuned)
Pixel Decoder: Upsamples ViT features to high resolution (interpolation + convs)
Transformer Decoder: DETR-style queries predict class + mask

At each layer: predicted masks → attention masks for next layer
Iteratively refines object boundaries


Typical Dense Tasks Transfer Learning Pipeline:
Feature Extraction ViT-L → ViT-Adapter (multi-scale features) → Mask2Former → masks + classes
Semantic Segmentation (ADE20K):

DINOv2 ViT-L backbone + ViT-Adapter + Mask2Former segmentation head.
59.3 Fine-tuned mIoU (Outperforms supervised pre-training mIoU 53.1)

Object Detection (COCO):

DINOv2 ViT-L backbone + ViT-Adapter + Mask R-CNN: 58.4 box AP (Outperforms supervised pre-training box AP 55.0)
SSL features excel at dense tasks

Video: DINOv2 features track across frames via k-NN (no temporal training needed).

title: 6  Self-Supervised Learning
text:
6.7 Summary and Interview Preparation

6.7.1 Core Concepts Checklist
Paradigms:

Invariance-based: Learn features invariant to augmentations
Reconstructive: Predict masked/corrupted input
Collapse problem and prevention strategies

Similarity-Based Methods:

Contrastive: Negatives prevent collapse (SimCLR, MoCo)
Clustering: Discrete assignments prevent collapse (DeepCluster, SwAV)
Self-Distillation: Asymmetry prevents collapse (BYOL, DINO)

Redundancy Reduction:

Decorrelate features: Cross-correlation → identity (Barlow Twins, VICReg)

Reconstructive:

MAE: 75% masking, asymmetric encoder-decoder
Why high mask ratio for images vs. BERT



6.7.2 Common Interview Questions

“Compare contrastive learning approaches—SimCLR vs. MoCo.”

SimCLR: In-batch negatives, needs large batches (4096-8192)
MoCo: Queue + momentum encoder, works with small batches (256)
Both ~70-71% linear probe, MoCo more memory-efficient

“How does BYOL work without negatives?”

Asymmetry: Predictor only in online network
Stop-gradient on target network (fixed targets)
Momentum update stabilizes target
SimSiam shows even momentum not strictly necessary

“Explain DINO’s centering mechanism.”

Prevents dimensional collapse (one feature dominating)
Subtract running mean of teacher outputs
Combined with sharp temperature (0.04) → confident pseudo-labels

“Barlow Twins vs. contrastive learning?”

Barlow: Decorrelate features (cross-correlation → identity)
Contrastive: Explicit negatives
Barlow: No negatives needed, works small batches, needs high-dim features

“Why does MAE use 75% masking?”

Images redundant (spatial continuity)
Low (15%) → trivial texture matching
High (75%) → forces semantic understanding
90%+ too hard (information loss)

“When to use invariance-based vs. reconstructive pre-training?”

Invariance: Better linear probe, good retrieval/few-shot
Reconstructive: Better dense tasks, compute-efficient, less augmentation-sensitive
Hybrid (DINOv2): Combines both → SOTA




6.7.3 Method Selection Guide
Choose Contrastive if:

Have compute for large batches
Care about linear probe performance
Need strong retrieval/similarity features

Choose Self-Distillation if:

Want simplicity (no negative sampling)
Using transformers (DINO family)
Need emergent segmentation

Choose Redundancy Reduction if:

Small batches, limited memory
Want interpretable objective
High-dimensional features available

Choose Reconstructive if:

Dense prediction is primary task
Limited augmentation expertise
Want compute efficiency (encoder sees 25% of tokens)



6.7.4 Company Context

Meta: DINOv2 (foundation model), MAE (LLAMA-vision backbone)
Google: SimCLR, ViT-MAE variants



6.7.5 Further Reading

Contrastive: SimCLR, MoCo
Self-Distillation: BYOL, DINO, DINOv2
Redundancy Reduction: Barlow Twins, VICReg
Reconstructive: MAE
Survey: Self-Supervised Learning in Vision


This completes Self-Supervised Learning—the paradigm enabling foundation models to learn from billions of unlabeled images, matching and exceeding supervised pre-training for transfer tasks.

title: Generative Models
text:
Discriminative vs. Generative Approaches
In machine learning, we can distinguish between two fundamental modeling paradigms:
Discriminative models focus on learning the conditional distribution \(p(y|x)\) or decision boundaries directly. Given an input \(x\), they predict the output \(y\) without modeling how the data itself is generated. Examples include most neural network classifiers, which learn to map inputs to labels efficiently.
Generative models learn the data distribution \(p(x)\) itself or the conditional distribution \(p(x|y)\). Rather than drawing a decision boundary, they model how the data itself is generated — enabling them to synthesize new samples, fill in missing information, or evaluate likelihoods of observations.

title: Generative Models
text:
The Generative Modeling Problem
Problem Statement: Given a dataset of images \(\mathcal{D} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_N\}\) drawn from an unknown distribution \(p_{\text{data}}(x)\), learn a model \(p_\theta(x)\) that approximates this distribution.
Learning such a distribution can be useful to:

Sample new images: \(x_{\text{new}} \sim p_\theta(x)\)
Evaluate likelihood: Compute \(p_\theta(x)\) for a given \(x\)
Learn representations: Extract meaningful latent structure

Extended Formulations:

Unconditional: \(p(x)\) — generate any image from learned distribution
Conditional: \(p(x \mid y)\) — generate image of class \(y\)
Latent variable: \(p(x \mid z)\) where \(z \sim p(z)\) — generate from learned latent space
Noisy conditional: \(p(x \mid y, \xi)\) where \(\xi\) is random noise

Before delving into architectures, it’s worth understanding why modeling data distributions is useful; and why generative models are central to many AI application.


Why Generative Models Matter
Key motivations:

Data synthesis: Generate realistic data to augment training sets or handle scarce/imbalanced classes.

Representation learning: Learn meaningful latent spaces that transfer across tasks — the foundation of self-supervised pretraining.

Likelihood modeling: Estimate \(p_\theta(x)\) for anomaly or out-of-distribution detection, compression, or uncertainty estimation.

Creative generation: Produce new visual content, designs, or scenes under controllable conditions — the core of text-to-image, video, and 3D generation systems.


In practice, generative modeling bridges analysis (understanding data) and creation (producing data) — a capability increasingly central to applied machine learning.



Classical Example: Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs)
GMMs illustrate core generative modeling ideas — latent variables, probabilistic assignments, and EM-style learning — which underpin modern neural generative models.
Setup: Model data as a mixture of \(K\) Gaussian components:
\[p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \cdot \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)\]

\(\pi_k\) = mixing coefficients (\(\sum_k \pi_k = 1\))

\(\mu_k\) = mean vector of cluster \(k\)

\(\Sigma_k\) = covariance matrix of cluster \(k\)

Each point \(x_i\) has an unobserved cluster assignment \(z_i\):
\[p(z_i = k) = \pi_k, \quad p(x_i \mid z_i = k) = \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)\]
Objective: Maximize log-likelihood:
\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)\]
EM Algorithm (soft cluster assignments):






Initialize parameters randomly (or via k-means)
Repeat until convergence:

E-step: Compute posterior responsibilities
\[\gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{\sum_j \pi_j \, \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}\]

Soft assignment: each point partially belongs to all clusters.

M-step: Update parameters using responsibilities
\[N_k = \sum_i \gamma_{ik}, \quad \mu_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_i \gamma_{ik} x_i\]
\[\Sigma_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_i \gamma_{ik} (x_i - \mu_k)(x_i - \mu_k)^\top, \quad \pi_k = \frac{N_k}{N}\]

Weighted updates reflect soft cluster assignments.





Generative Process:






I. Sample cluster: \(z \sim \text{Categorical}(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_K)\)
II. Sample point: \(x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \Sigma_z)\)



GMMs generalize K-means by using soft probabilistic assignments and flexible cluster shapes.



Connection to Neural Generative Models
GMMs teach the key concepts of latent structure and probabilistic inference that scale to modern neural generative models, which generalize them with the following modifications:

Latent variables → continuous latent codes in VAEs/GANs

Posterior inference → encoder networks (amortized inference in VAEs)

EM-style learning → alternating inference and generative updates (encoder + decoder)

Likelihood-based learning → ELBO maximization in VAEs

Limitation: GMMs do not scale to high-dimensional images due to

parameter explosion (Covariance matrix is \(O(d^2)\) parameters, d the number of image pixels)
lack of spatial structure exploitation — solved via convolutions and latent representations.




Chapter Roadmap
Deep Learning Generative Models — different approaches are shown in Figure 1:






Figure 1: Taxonomy of deep learning generative models. Likelihood-based methods (VAEs, Flows, Autoregressive) explicitly model \(p(x)\), while implicit methods (GANs) learn to sample without density estimation. Diffusion models combine both paradigms.



From this taxonomy (Figure 1), we focus on three major families:
7.1: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)

Latent variable models with learned encoders/decoders
Variational inference and the evidence lower bound (ELBO)
Applications: Disentangled representations, controllable generation

§7.2: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)

Adversarial training framework: Generator vs. Discriminator
StyleGAN architecture and latent space manipulation; conditional GANs
Applications: High-fidelity image synthesis, style transfer

§7.3: Diffusion Models

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs)
Latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion architecture)
Applications: Text-to-image generation, video generation, impainting

These three paradigms are often compared in terms of a trade-off known as the generative trilemma.
This concept suggests that a generative model can typically only satisfy two of the following three desirable properties: high-quality samples, high diversity (mode coverage), and fast sampling speed. The choice between VAEs, GANs, and Diffusion Models often depends on which of these aspects is prioritized for a given application. This trade-off is summarized in the following diagram (Figure 2):






Figure 2: Trade-offs between GANs (green), VAEs (blue), and Diffusion Models (purple). Each paradigm prioritizes two of the three competing properties: high sample quality, fast sampling, and mode coverage (diversity).



Note on Coverage: Autoregressive models introduced in §6.6 (Self-Supervised Learning) under masked prediction objectives and are not revisited here (TODO: Overview of the classical work of PixelCNN, PixelRNN, or recent approches such as MaskGIT). Normalizing Flows, while theoretically elegant, have been largely superseded by diffusion models in practice and are mentioned only briefly.

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
7.1 From Dimensionality Reduction to Generative Models
The Autoencoder Foundation
Dimensionality Reduction seeks encoder \(e: \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}^d\) and decoder \(d: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D\) (with \(d \ll D\)) that minimize reconstruction error:
\[(e^*, d^*) = \arg\min_{(e,d) \in \mathcal{E} \times \mathcal{D}} \sum_{x_i \in \mathcal{D}} \|x_i - d(e(x_i))\|^2\]
Linear Case - Principal Component Analysis (PCA):
When encoder and decoder are restricted to linear transformations (no activation functions), the optimal solution is given by Principal Component Analysis:
Result: PCA provides the optimal \(d\)-dimensional linear subspace minimizing reconstruction error.
Non-Linear Case - Autoencoders:
Replace linear transformations with neural networks:
Training: Minimize reconstruction loss \(\mathcal{L} = \|x - \hat{x}\|^2\) via backpropagation.
Problem for Generation: Latent space is irregular—random samples \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) often produce nonsensical reconstructions.
Desired Properties for Generative Latent Space:
Standard Autoencoders Fail: Without regularization, encoder maps data to arbitrary regions, leaving gaps (holes) in latent space.
Variational Autoencoders Solution: Regularize latent space during training to enforce these properties.

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
Compute covariance matrix \(\Sigma = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(x_i - \bar{x})^\top\)
Find top \(d\) eigenvectors \(\{v_1, \ldots, v_d\}\) with largest eigenvalues
Encoder: \(e(x) = V^\top (x - \bar{x})\) where \(V = [v_1, \ldots, v_d]\)
Decoder: \(d(z) = Vz + \bar{x}\)











\(\textbf{Encoder:} \quad x \;\rightarrow\; \text{CNN/MLP} \;\rightarrow\; z \in \mathbb{R}^d \;(\text{bottleneck})\\\) \(\textbf{Decoder:} \quad z \;\rightarrow\; \text{Transposed CNN/MLP} \;\rightarrow\; \hat{x} \in \mathbb{R}^D\)










Figure 7.1: Autoencoder Architecture: The encoder (\(\mathbf{e}\)) and decoder (\(\mathbf{d}\)) create a dimension bottleneck by compressing the input \(\mathbf{x}\) into a latent representation \(\mathbf{z}\). The model is trained to minimize the reconstruction error (typically MSE or \(\ell_2\)-norm) between \(\mathbf{x}\) and the reconstructed output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\). Adapted from Rocca (Rocca 2021).







Continuity: Nearby points in latent space → similar generated outputs

\(\|z_1 - z_2\| \text{ small} \Rightarrow \|d(z_1) - d(z_2)\| \text{ small}\)

Completeness: Every point in latent space → meaningful output

For any \(z\) in relevant region, \(d(z)\) should be a plausible image















Figure 7.2: Regular vs. Irregular Variational Autoencoder latent spaces. The VAE’s regularization produces a continuous latent manifold where all points decode to plausible samples. Adapted from Rocca (Rocca 2021).

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
7.2 Probabilistic Formulation
Generative Model:

Sample latent: \(z \sim p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\)
Generate data: \(x \sim p_\theta(x|z)\) (learned decoder)

Goal: Maximize likelihood \(p_\theta(x)\) for observed data, which is intractable (it requires \(\int p_\theta(x|z)p(z)dz\))
Solution: Introduce approximate posterior \(q_\phi(z|x)\) (encoder), and






TipDerive Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO):





\[\text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi; x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)]}_{\text{Reconstruction}} - \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}(q_\phi(z|x) \| p(z))}_{\text{Regularization}}\]
Starting from log-likelihood:
\[\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x|z) p(z) dz\]
Multiply by \(\frac{q_\phi(z|x)}{q_\phi(z|x)} = 1\) inside integral:
\[= \log \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} \left[ \frac{p_\theta(x|z) p(z)}{q_\phi(z|x)} \right]\]
Apply Jensen’s inequality (\(\log \mathbb{E}[X] \geq \mathbb{E}[\log X]\)):
\[\geq \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)} \left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(x|z) p(z)}{q_\phi(z|x)} \right]\]
Rearrange:
\[= \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) \| p(z))\]
This is the ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund):
\[\text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi; x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)]}_{\text{Reconstruction term}} - \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}(q_\phi(z|x) \| p(z))}_{\text{Regularization term}}\]



Interpretation:

Reconstruction: Encourages decoder to reconstruct input accurately (like autoencoder loss)
KL Regularization: Enforces continuity/completeness keeping \(q_\phi(z|x)\) close to \(p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0,I)\)

Why “Lower Bound”?
 Since \(\log p_\theta(x) = \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi; x) + \text{KL}(q_\phi \| p_\theta(z|x))
\geq \text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi; x)\quad
(\text{ KL} \geq 0)\),  a good encoder (small KL) makes maximizing ELBO ≈ maximizing likelihood

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
7.3 Architecture and Training
Network Architecture:

Encoder \(q_\phi(z|x)\) outputs distribution parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) (not a single point): \[x \;\rightarrow\; \text{CNN} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Flatten} \;\rightarrow\; \text{FC} \;\rightarrow\; [\mu(x), \log \sigma^2(x)] \in \mathbb{R}^d\]

\[q_\phi(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(z; \mu_\phi(x), \sigma_\phi^2(x) I)\]

Decoder \(p_\theta(x|z)\) reconstructs from latent code: \[p_\theta(x|z) = \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_\theta(z), \sigma^2 I)\]

\[z \;\rightarrow\; \text{FC} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Reshape} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Transposed CNN} \;\rightarrow\; \hat{x} \in \mathbb{R}^D\]
Note: Encoder outputs log-variance to ensure \(\sigma^2 > 0\)
(even if the network outputs negative values for \(\log \sigma^2\), \(\sigma^2 = \exp(\log \sigma^2)\) is still positive).
Decoder is modeled as a Gaussian with fixed variance, making its reconstruction loss equivalent to MSE: \(\log p_\theta(x|z) \propto -\|\hat{x} - x\|^2\).

Loss Function:
Minimize negative ELBO: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = \underbrace{\|x - \hat{x}\|^2}_{\text{Reconstruction}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^d \left(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - \log \sigma_j^2 - 1\right)}_{\text{KL regularization}}\]
The regularization term is the closed-form for KL-divergence of two gaussians \(\text{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \| \mathcal{N}(0, I))\)
The overall structure of the VAE—encoder, sampling, and decoder—and the loss components are illustrated in Figure 7.3 .






Figure 7.3: VAE architecture and loss. The encoder outputs a Gaussian \(( \mu, \sigma )\), from which \(z\) is sampled and decoded to reconstruct \(\hat{x}\). The loss balances reconstruction fidelity and latent regularization via KL divergence. Adapted from Rocca (Rocca 2021).




Reparameterization Trick:
Problem: Sampling \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) is not differentiable—cannot backpropagate through random sampling.
Solution: Reparameterize as \(z = \mu(x) + \sigma(x) \odot \epsilon\) where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\).

Randomness is in \(\epsilon\) (sampled once, treated as constant).
Gradients flow through \(\mu(x)\) and \(\sigma(x)\).







Figure 7.4: Reparameterization trick. Left: Sampling directly from \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) blocks gradients.
Right: Reparameterization moves sampling to fixed \(\epsilon\), allowing gradients to flow through \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). Adapted from Rocca (Rocca 2021).




Training Algorithm:
for each batch x:
    # Encoder: predict distribution parameters
    μ, log_σ² = encoder(x)
    σ = exp(0.5 * log_σ²)
    
    # Reparameterization trick
    ε ~ N(0, I)
    z = μ + σ ⊙ ε
    
    # Decoder: reconstruct
    x̂ = decoder(z)
    
    # Loss
    reconstruction_loss = ||x - x̂||²
    kl_loss = 0.5 * sum(μ² + σ² - log σ² - 1)
    loss = reconstruction_loss + kl_loss
    
    # Backpropagation
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
Generation Process:
# Sample from prior
z ~ N(0, I)

# Decode
x̂ = decoder(z)
No encoder needed at generation time!

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
7.4 Variants and Extensions
Conditional VAE (CVAE, 2015)
Idea: Condition generation on class label \(y\).
Modification:

Encoder: \(q_\phi(z|x, y)\) (takes both \(x\) and \(y\) as input)
Decoder: \(p_\theta(x|z, y)\) (generates \(x\) conditioned on \(z\) and \(y\))
Prior: \(p(z|y)\) (can be class-specific)

Loss: Same ELBO structure, but conditioned on \(y\):
\[\text{ELBO}(\theta, \phi; x, y) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x,y)}[\log p_\theta(x|z, y)] - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x, y) \| p(z|y))\]
Generation: Sample class \(y\), then \(z \sim p(z|y)\), then \(x \sim p_\theta(x|z, y)\).
Application: Generate images of specific classes (e.g., “generate a digit 7”).

β-VAE (2017): Disentangled Representations
Motivation: Standard VAE often learns entangled representations where multiple latent dimensions change together.
Modification: Add weight \(\beta > 1\) to KL term:
\[\text{ELBO}_{\beta\text{-VAE}} = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - \beta \cdot \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) \| p(z))\]
Effect:

\(\beta > 1\): Stronger regularization → more disentangled (but blurrier reconstructions)
\(\beta = 1\): Standard VAE
\(\beta < 1\): Less regularization → sharper reconstructions (but entangled)

Typical values: \(\beta \in [2, 10]\) for disentanglement tasks.
Applications: Interpretable latent factors (e.g., face attributes: pose, lighting, identity separated).

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
7.5 VQ-VAE: Vector Quantized VAE
Motivation: Standard VAE uses continuous latent space. VQ-VAE uses discrete latent codes (like words in language).
Key Idea: Replace continuous \(z \in \mathbb{R}^d\) with discrete codebook indices.
Architecture:






Figure 7.5: The architecture of a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE). An encoder E(x) maps the input x to a continuous latent space. The Quantization step then maps the latent vectors to the nearest vector from a discrete, learned Codebook of embeddings, forming the discrete latent code z_q(x). This discrete code is then passed to the decoder D(z_q(x)) to reconstruct the image. The diagram on the right illustrates the nearest-neighbor lookup in the embedding space.




Codebook: Learnable embedding table \(\mathcal{E} = \{e_1, \ldots, e_K\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) with \(K\) vectors (e.g., \(K=512\)).
Encoding

Encoder outputs spatial feature map: \(E(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d}\)

Quantization

For each spatial location \((i,j)\), find nearest codebook vector: \[k_{i,j} = \arg\min_l \|E(x)_{i,j} - e_l\|_2\]
Replace with codebook vector: \(z_q(x)_{i,j} = e_{k_{i,j}}\)

Decoding: \(\hat{x} = D(z_q(x))\)


Loss:
\[\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\|x - D(z_q(x))\|_2^2}_{\text{Reconstruction}} + \underbrace{\|\text{sg}[E(x)] - z_q(x)\|_2^2}_{\text{Codebook (VQ)}} + \underbrace{\beta \|E(x) - \text{sg}[z_q(x)]\|_2^2}_{\text{Commitment}}\]
where \(\text{sg}[\cdot]\) is stop-gradient operator.
Three Loss Terms:

Reconstruction Loss: Updates encoder and decoder (standard autoencoder loss)
Codebook Loss (VQ):Updates the codebook embeddings \(e_k\) to match the encoder outputs they represent.
Commitment Loss: Updates the encoder outputs to stay close to their assigned codebook vectors, stabilizing quantization and preventing the encoder from drifting.

Weight \(\beta = 0.25\) typically

Alternative - EMA Update (instead of VQ loss):
Update codebook vectors via exponential moving average (like k-means):

\[N_k \leftarrow N_k \cdot \gamma + (1-\gamma) \sum_{i,j} \mathbb{1}[k_{i,j} = k]\] \[e_k \leftarrow \frac{N_k \cdot \gamma \cdot e_k + \sum_{i,j:\, k_{i,j}=k} E(x)_{i,j}}{N_k}\]

Straight-Through Estimator:
Problem: \(\arg\min\) operation (nearest neighbor) is not differentiable.
Solution: In backward pass, copy gradient from decoder input to encoder output: \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial E(x)} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_q(x)}\]
Intuition: Pretend quantization is identity function during backpropagation.

Advantages of VQ-VAE:

No posterior collapse: There’s no KL term forcing \(q(z|x)\) toward a standard Normal prior, so the latent codes retain information about \(x\).
Compatibility with autoregressive models: Prior \(p(z)\) can be learned with PixelCNN/Transformer
Better codebook utilization: All \(K\) codes typically get used (vs. continuous VAE where some dimensions are ignored)

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
7.6 VQ-VAE-2: Hierarchical Discrete Latents
Motivation: Single-scale VQ-VAE struggles with both global structure and fine details.
Solution: Hierarchical latent codes at multiple resolutions.
Architecture:

Two-Level Hierarchical Encoder:

Top-level encoder: \(x \to z_{\text{top}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H/32 \times W/32 \times d}\) (low resolution, global features)
Bottom-level encoder: \(x \to z_{\text{bottom}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H/16 \times W/16 \times d}\) (high resolution, local features)

Both quantized with separate codebooks (512 vectors each).
Decoder: Takes both quantized representations: \[\hat{x} = D(z_q^{\text{top}}, z_q^{\text{bottom}})\] Top-level quantized (codebook) representations are upsampled to match the spatial resolution of the bottom-level codes and concatenated along the channel dimension.


Two-Stage Training:

Stage 1 - Train VQ-VAE :
Trains the hierarchical encoder–decoder and two codebooks using reconstruction and vq losses.
→ The trained model can encode and reconstruct inputs, but cannot yet generate new samples.
Stage 2 - Train Prior Models:
Trains autoregressive models over the discrete latent variables using PixelCNN or Transformers:

Top prior: \(p(z_{\text{top}})\) (unconditional)

Train autoregressive model on top-level codes

Bottom prior: \(p(z_{\text{bottom}} | z_{\text{top}})\) (conditional)

Train autoregressive model on bottom-level codes, conditioned on top codes


→ Sample new data samples by drawing discrete codes from the learned priors, then decoding them through the VQ-VAE decoder (see Generation Process below).

Generation Process:
# Sample top-level codes autoregressively
z_top ~ p_top  # using trained PixelCNN

# Sample bottom-level codes conditioned on top
z_bottom ~ p_bottom(· | z_top)  # using conditional PixelCNN

# Decode to image
x = Decoder(z_top, z_bottom)

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
7.7 Practical Considerations
Architecture Choices:

Encoder/Decoder Depth: Deeper networks → better features, harder to train

Start simple: 3-4 conv layers each
Advanced: ResNet-style blocks

Latent Dimension: Trade-off between compression and reconstruction

Too small (\(d < 10\)): Poor reconstructions
Too large (\(d > 512\)): KL collapse (posterior collapses to prior)
Typical: \(d \in [32, 256]\)

KL Annealing: Gradually increase KL weight from 0 to 1 during training

Prevents early KL collapse
Allows decoder to learn before enforcing strong regularization



Training Issues:
1. Posterior Collapse: KL term goes to 0, model ignores latent code

Symptom: Decoder generates always the same output regardless of \(z\)
Solutions: KL annealing; free bits (minimum KL per dimension, i.e. optimize: \(\max(\text{KL}_j, \lambda)\) instead of \(\text{KL}_j\)); or \(\beta\)-VAE with \(\beta < 1\) initially

2. Blurry Reconstructions: MSE loss averages over modes

Symptom: Images look blurry compared to input
Cause: MSE loss \(= \mathbb{E}[\|x - \hat{x}\|^2]\) encourages averaging
Partial solutions: Perceptual loss (VGG similarity in deep feature space between input \(x\) and reconstruction \(\hat{x}\)); adversarial loss (VAE-GAN hybrid)

3. KL-Reconstruction Trade-off: Balancing two loss terms

High KL weight → regular latent space but poor reconstructions
Low KL weight → good reconstructions but irregular latent space
Solutions: Grid search for optimal weighting; β-VAE


Technical property:
VAEs use continuous latent spaces, allowing smooth interpolation and controllable generation: \[z_{\text{interp}} = (1-\alpha) z_1 + \alpha z_2, \quad \alpha \in [0,1],\] where interpolating between latent codes \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) produces meaningful intermediate output images.

title: 7  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
7.8 Summary and Interview Preparation
Core Concepts Checklist:
Mathematical Foundation:

ELBO derivation from KL divergence
Why ELBO is lower bound on log-likelihood
Closed-form KL for Gaussian distributions
Reparameterization trick and why it’s needed

Architecture:

Encoder outputs distribution parameters \((\mu, \sigma^2)\)
Decoder is probabilistic: \(p_\theta(x|z)\)
Prior \(p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\)

VAE Variants:

β-VAE for disentanglement
CVAE for conditional generation
VQ-VAE: discrete codebook latents
VQ-VAE-2: hierarchical multi-scale

Training:

Two-term loss: reconstruction + KL
Posterior collapse problem
KL annealing strategy


Common Interview Questions:
1. “Derive the VAE loss function (ELBO).”
Answer: Start with log-likelihood: \(\log p(x) = \log \int p(x|z)p(z)dz\)
Introduce \(q(z|x)\): \(= \log \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}\left[\frac{p(x|z)p(z)}{q(z|x)}\right]\)
Jensen’s inequality: \(\geq \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}\left[\log p(x|z)\right] - \text{KL}(q(z|x)\|p(z))\)
This is ELBO. Maximizing ELBO = maximizing lower bound on likelihood.

2. “Explain the reparameterization trick and why it’s necessary.”
Answer: Problem: Sampling \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) is not differentiable—can’t backprop through stochastic node.
Solution: Reparameterize as \(z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon\) where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\).
Now \(\epsilon\) is constant (sampled once), and gradients flow through \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). Enables end-to-end training with backpropagation.

3. “Why do VAE reconstructions tend to be blurry?”
Answer: Cause: MSE loss \(\mathbb{E}[\|x - \hat{x}\|^2]\) encourages decoder to output mean of conditional distribution \(p(x|z)\).
When \(p(x|z)\) is multimodal (multiple valid reconstructions), mean is blurry average.
Solutions:

Perceptual loss (VGG features instead of pixels)
Adversarial loss (VAE-GAN hybrid)
Better decoder distributions (Mixture of Logistics)


4. “VAE vs. GAN—when to use each?”
Answer:
VAE:

✓ Stable training
✓ Computable likelihood (useful for anomaly detection)
✓ Good mode coverage
✓ Fast inference (encoder available)
✗ Blurry samples (MSE loss)

GAN:

✓ Sharp, high-quality samples
✗ Unstable training (mode collapse)
✗ No encoder (can’t infer \(z\) from \(x\) easily)
✗ No likelihood computation

Use VAE when: Need likelihood, stability, representation learning Use GAN when: Need highest quality samples, don’t need encoder

5. “Explain VQ-VAE and why it’s useful.”
Answer: VQ-VAE uses discrete codebook latents instead of continuous:

Encoder outputs feature map, each spatial location quantized to nearest codebook vector
No posterior collapse (discrete codes)
Compatible with autoregressive priors (learn \(p(z)\) with PixelCNN)

Why useful:

Foundation for DALL-E (VQ-VAE + GPT generates images)
Better than continuous for capturing discrete modes
Used in Stable Diffusion latent space compression


6. “What is posterior collapse in VAEs and how to fix it?”
Answer: Posterior collapse: KL term → 0, \(q(z|x) \approx p(z)\).
Decoder ignores \(z\), generates from marginal \(p(x)\) only.
Causes:

Decoder too powerful (can model \(p(x)\) without \(z\))
KL weight too high initially

Solutions:

KL annealing: Start with low β, gradually increase
Free bits: Minimum KL per dimension (don’t push below threshold)
β-VAE with β < 1 initially, then increase
Weaker decoder: Limit capacity to force latent usage

DALL-E uses VQ-VAE for discrete tokens + GPT for prior
Exploring VAEs for representation learning

Stability AI:

Stable Diffusion uses VAE encoder/decoder (compress to latent space)
Diffusion in latent space (not pixel space)

VQ-VAE-2 research
Hierarchical VAEs for video (VideoGPT)

VAE-based compression for videos
Research on disentangled representations (β-VAE)

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
8.1 Introduction
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) learn to generate data through a two-player game between competing neural networks. Unlike VAEs which use explicit density modeling, GANs learn an implicit generative model through adversarial training.
Core Idea: Train two networks in opposition:
Key Insight: The generator never sees real data directly—it only receives gradients from the discriminator’s judgment. This indirect supervision produces remarkably sharp, high-quality samples.

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
Generator \(G\): Creates fake samples to fool the discriminator
Discriminator \(D\): Distinguishes real data from generated fakes




8.1.1 Minmax Game Formulation
Generator and discriminator play a minimax game with value function \(V(G, D)\):
\[\min_G \max_D V(D, G) = \min_G \max_D \Big(\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]\Big)\]
Discriminator’s objective:
Maximize \(V(D, G)\);   by correctly classifying real data (\(D(x) \to 1\)) and fake data (\(D(G(z)) \to 0\)).
Generator’s objective:
Minimize \(V(D, G)\);   by fooling the discriminator (\(D(G(z)) \to 0\)).



8.1.2 Architecture Components
Generator \(G: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{X}\):

Input: Latent code \(z \sim p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) (typically)
Output: Generated sample \(\hat{x} = G(z) \in \mathbb{R}^D\)
Architecture: Transposed convolutions (images) or MLPs (tabular)

\[z \to \text{FC} \to \text{Reshape} \to \text{TransposedConv} \times N \to \text{Tanh} \to \hat{x}\]
Discriminator \(D: \mathcal{X} \to [0,1]\):

Input: Sample \(x\) (real or fake)
Output: Probability that \(x\) is real: \(D(x) \in [0,1]\)
Architecture: Convolutional network (images) or MLPs

\[x \to \text{Conv} \times N \to \text{Flatten} \to \text{FC} \to \text{Sigmoid} \to D(x)\]



8.1.3 Training Algorithm
Alternating optimization—train discriminator and generator in turns:
for epoch in epochs:
    # Train Discriminator (k steps, typically k=1)
    for _ in range(k):
        # Sample real data
        x_real ~ p_data(x)
        
        # Sample noise and generate fakes
        z ~ p(z)
        x_fake = G(z)
        
        # Discriminator loss (binary cross-entropy)
        L_D = -[log D(x_real) + log(1 - D(x_fake))]
        
        # Update discriminator
        θ_D ← θ_D - η ∇_θD L_D
    
    # Train Generator (1 step)
    z ~ p(z)
    x_fake = G(z)
    
    # Generator loss (non-saturating)
    L_G = -log D(G(z))
    
    # Update generator
    θ_G ← θ_G - η ∇_θG L_G
Key design choice: Update discriminator more frequently (\(k\) times) per generator update to maintain discriminator strength.

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
8.2 Unconditional Image Generation

8.2.1 DCGAN (Deep Convolutional GAN, 2015)
Key contribution: Stable architecture guidelines for training GANs on images.
Architecture principles: 1. Replace pooling layers with strided convolutions (discriminator) and transposed convolutions (generator) 2. Use batch normalization in both networks (except generator output and discriminator input) 3. Remove fully connected hidden layers 4. Use ReLU in generator (except output: Tanh) 5. Use LeakyReLU in discriminator
Generator architecture (for 64×64 images):
z (100) → FC(4×4×1024) → Reshape
  → TransposedConv(512, 4×4, stride=2) → BN → ReLU  # 8×8
  → TransposedConv(256, 4×4, stride=2) → BN → ReLU  # 16×16
  → TransposedConv(128, 4×4, stride=2) → BN → ReLU  # 32×32
  → TransposedConv(3, 4×4, stride=2) → Tanh          # 64×64
Impact: Enabled stable training, became foundation for future GAN research.



8.2.2 WGAN (Wasserstein GAN ,2017)
Motivation: Address training instability through better distance metric.
Key idea: Instead of Jensen-Shannon divergence, use Wasserstein distance (Earth Mover’s Distance):
\[W(p_r, p_g) = \sup_{\|f\|_L \leq 1} \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_r}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g}[f(x)]\]
WGAN objective: \[\min_G \max_{D \in \mathcal{D}} \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[D(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[D(G(z))]\]
Key differences from standard GAN:



Aspect
Standard GAN
WGAN




Discriminator output
Sigmoid (probability)
Linear (score)


Loss
Binary cross-entropy
Wasserstein distance


Constraint
None
1-Lipschitz


Stability
Sensitive to hyperparameters
More stable



Advantages: Provides meaningful gradients even when distributions don’t overlap, more stable training.
Enforcing Lipschitz constraint: The Wasserstein GAN optimizes the Earth-Mover distance, which requires the critic to be 1-Lipschitz. This smoothness constraint is essential for the distance to be valid (via the Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality). The original WGAN enforces this constraint by clipping the critic’s weights, a simple but crude way to bound the gradients.
# Enforcing 1-Lipschitz constraint (original WGAN)
for p in discriminator.parameters():
    p.data.clamp_(-0.01, 0.01)
Problems with weight clipping:

Limits discriminator model capacity
Can lead to unstable or flat value surfaces
Slows Convergence




8.2.3 WGAN-GP (2017)
Improvement: Replace weight clipping with gradient penalty.
Gradient penalty: \[\lambda \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x} \sim p_{\hat{x}}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]\]
for any interpolated point \(\hat{x}\) between a real data sample and a generated sample
(i.e., convex combinations of the form \(\hat{x} = \epsilon x + (1-\epsilon)G(z), \, \epsilon \in [0,1]\)).
Complete loss: \[\mathcal{L}_D = \mathbb{E}_z[D(G(z))] - \mathbb{E}_x[D(x)] + \lambda \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]\]
Benefits: Better gradient behavior, no weight clipping issues.
Standard practice for Wasserstein GANs (typically \(\lambda = 10\)).

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
8.3 Conditional Image Generation

8.3.1 Conditional GAN (cGAN, 2014)
Idea: Condition both networks on labels \(y\):
\[\min_G \max_D \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\log D(x|y)] + \mathbb{E}_{z,y}[\log(1 - D(G(z|y)|y))]\]
Implementation:
# Generator
y_embedded = embedding(y)
z_cond = concat([z, y_embedded])
x = G(z_cond)

# Discriminator  
x_cond = concat([x, y_embedded])
score = D(x_cond)
Applications:

Class-conditional image generation (ImageNet)
Text-to-image synthesis
Image-to-image translation (pix2pix)
Super-resolution


Having covered conditional GANs, we now move to advances in unconditional high-resolution image generation, which ultimately led to StyleGAN.

Prior to StyleGAN, Progressive GAN introduced progressive growing — a key technique that allowed stable training at very high resolutions (up to 1024×1024), and was later adopted in early versions of StyleGAN.


8.3.2 Progressive GAN (2017)
Key idea: Train generator & discriminator by gradually increasing resolution
(4×4 → 8×8 → 16×16 → … → 1024×1024)
Fade-in mechanism: Smooth transition when adding layers
x_lowres = upsample(prev_block(x))
x_highres = new_block(x)
x = α * x_highres + (1 - α) * x_lowres  # α: ramps from 0→1
Benefits:

Stable training at high resolution
Faster convergence
Much sharper high-resolution results than prior GANs




8.3.3 StyleGAN (2018-2019)
Key innovation: Style-based generator with explicit control over image features at different scales.
Architecture overview:
1. Mapping Network \(f: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{W}\):

8-layer MLP maps \(z\in \mathcal{Z}\) to disentangled latent \(w \in \mathcal{W}\)

2. Synthesis Network: Generates image from \(w\)

Starts from learned constant tensor (not latent vector)
Progressive upsampling; each layer modulated by style vector \(w\) through Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN)

AdaIN (Style Modulation): Applies style controls by normalizing activations and re-scaling them with learned scale/bias from \(w\): \[\text{AdaIN}(x_i, y) = y_{s,i} \frac{x_i - \mu(x_i)}{\sigma(x_i)} + y_{b,i}\]
3. Hierarchical Style Control:

Coarse (4×4–8×8): pose, face shape
Middle (16×16–32×32): facial features, hair
Fine (64×64–1024×1024): colors, pores, micro-structure

Style mixing regularization: Inject different \(w\) vectors at different layers to encourage disentanglement and prevent the network from encoding all variation in early layers.
4. Noise Injection: Per-pixel Gaussian noise at each layer → stochastic realism (hair strands, pores, skin variation)
x = conv(x)
x = x + noise * learned_weight  # Uncorrelated Gaussian noise
x = activation(x)
Results: State-of-the-art 1024×1024 image quality (FID ~3 on FFHQ faces dataset).
StyleGAN2 later removed progressive growing and improved normalization to eliminate artifacts.

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
8.4 Image-to-Image Translation
Goal: Learn a mapping between two visual domains \(X\) and \(Y\). Given input \(x \in X\), generate \(y \in Y\).

Paired setting: explicit aligned pairs \((x_i, y_i)\) are available
Unpaired setting: only samples from each distribution, no direct correspondences


8.4.1 Pix2Pix (2016) — Paired Translation
Setting: Learn \((G: X \rightarrow Y)\) with paired examples \((x, y)\).

Generator: U-Net (skip connections preserve spatial details)
Discriminator: PatchGAN (classifies local patches as real/fake)

Loss: \[\mathcal{L}_\text{Pix2Pix} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{L1}}\]

\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{L1}} = \mathbb{E}[\|y - G(x)\|_1]\)
\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}} = \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\log D(x,y)] + \mathbb{E}_{x}[\log(1 - D(x, G(x)))]\)
GAN loss encourages realistic textures; L1 keeps output close to the paired target.

Applications: Conditional generation across paired domains, including:

edges → photos
labels → scenes (semantic → realistic)
image colorization
super-resolution



8.4.2 CycleGAN (2017) — Unpaired Translation
Setting: Unsupervised translation (no paired data). Learn mappings both ways: \[
G: X \rightarrow Y, \quad F: Y \rightarrow X
\]
Key idea — Cycle Consistency: Translating forward then back should reconstruct the original:
\[
F(G(x)) \approx x, \quad G(F(y)) \approx y
\]
Loss: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}(G) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}(F) +
\lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{cyc}} +
\lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{id}}
\]
Adversarial loss:   enforces that translating to the other domain and back recovers the original image

\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}(G)=
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_{\text{data}}(y)}[(D_Y(y) - 1)^2]+
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[D_Y(G(x))^2]\)
\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}(F)=
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[(D_X(x) - 1)^2]+
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_{\text{data}}(y)}[D_X(F(y))^2]\)

Cycle Loss:   enforces that translating to the other domain and back recovers the original image

\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{cyc}} =
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[\|F(G(x)) - x\|_1] +
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y)}[\|G(F(y)) - y\|_1]\)

Identity Loss:   preserves content when input already resembles target domain

\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{id}} \,\ = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y)} \left[ \lVert G(y) - y \rVert_1 \right]+
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} \left[ \lVert F(x) - x \rVert_1 \right]\)

Applications: Cross-domain translation without paired supervision, e.g.,

season transfer
horse ↔︎ zebra
apples ↔︎ oranges
photo ↔︎ painting style

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
8.5 Evaluation Metrics
Evaluating generative models is challenging because we cannot compute exact likelihoods for GANs. Instead, we rely on proxy metrics that measure different aspects of generation quality.

8.5.1 Inception Score (IS)
Motivation: Good generated images should satisfy two properties:

Sharpness: Each image should clearly belong to one class → \(p(y|x)\) has low entropy
Diversity: Generated images should cover many classes → marginal \(p(y)\) has high entropy

Formula: \[\text{IS} = \exp\left(\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g}[\text{KL}(p(y|x) \| p(y))]\right)\]

\(p(y|x)\) is Inception-v3’s predicted class distribution,
\(p(y) = \mathbb{E}_x[p(y|x)]\) is the marginal.

Intuition:
\[\ln(\text{IS}) = \underbrace{H(y)}_{\text{diversity across dataset}} -
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[H(y|x)]}_{\text{avg. uncertainty per image}}\]






TipMathematical Derivation (click to expand)





\[\text{KL}(p(y|x) \| p(y)) = \sum_y p(y|x) \log p(y|x) - \sum_y p(y|x) \log p(y)\] \[= -H(y|x) - \sum_y p(y|x) \log p(y)\]
Taking expectation over \(x \sim p_g\): \[\mathbb{E}_x[\text{KL}(p(y|x) \| p(y))] = -\mathbb{E}_x[H(y|x)] + H(y)\]
Therefore: \[\boxed{\ln(\text{IS}(G)) = H(y) - \mathbb{E}_{x}[H(y|x)]}\]





High \(H(y)\): Generator produces many different classes (diversity)
Low \(H(y|x)\): Each image is sharp and recognizable (quality)

Critical limitation:

Depends on Inception network
IS evaluates \(p_g\) in isolation—not comparing it to real distribution \(p_{\text{data}}\).
A generator could game a high IS by:

Producing a single perfect image per class (high \(H(y)\), low \(\mathbb{E}[H(y|x)]\))
Memorizing training set (Overfitting)
Generating unrealistic but sharp images (Deviation from real distribution)





8.5.2 Fréchet Inception Distance (FID)
Measure distance between real and generated distributions in feature space.
Key difference:

IS: Evaluates \(p_g\) in isolation (requires only generated samples)
FID: Compares \(p_g\) to \(p_{\text{data}}\) (requires both real and generated samples)

Method:

Extract features from Inception-v3 (before final classification layer) for real and generated images
Assume feature distributions follow multivariate Gaussians:
Compute Fréchet distance (Wasserstein-2 distance between Gaussians)

Formula: \[\text{FID}(p_r, p_g) = \|\mu_r - \mu_g\|^2 + \text{Tr}\left(\Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2(\Sigma_r \Sigma_g)^{1/2}\right)\]

\(\mu_r, \Sigma_r\) are mean and covariance of real data features
\(\mu_g, \Sigma_g\) are mean and covariance of generated data features

Interpretation of terms:

Lower FID is better: closer match to real data. FID = 0 when distributions are identical.
\(\|\mu_r - \mu_g\|^2\):   Distance between feature means.

Measures how far the average generated sample is from the average real sample in feature space (if this term is large, the generator is producing images that, on average, look different from real ones - wrong global appearance, color tone, style bias, etc..).


\(\text{Tr}(\Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2\sqrt{\Sigma_r \Sigma_g})\):   Difference in covariances.

Measures if generated samples have similar diversity and correlations as real data
Penalizes mode collapse (when generator produces only a few types of images).


Best practice: Use FID as primary metric (measures distance to real distribution), IS for quick checks only.



8.5.3 Precision and Recall
FID is a single number that doesn’t distinguish between quality and diversity failures.
Precision and Recall separately measure quality from diversity:

Precision: Fraction of generated samples that are realistic (quality)
Recall: Fraction of real data modes covered by generator (diversity)

Computation (using k-NN in feature space):
# Extract Inception features
real_features = Inception(real_images)
fake_features = Inception(generated_images)

# Precision: fraction of fake samples with real neighbor nearby
distances_fake_to_real = knn_distance(fake_features, real_features, k=3)
precision = (distances_fake_to_real < threshold).mean()

# Recall: fraction of real samples with fake neighbor nearby
distances_real_to_fake = knn_distance(real_features, fake_features, k=3)
recall = (distances_real_to_fake < threshold).mean()
Diagnosis:

High precision, low recall → mode collapse
Low precision, high recall → diverse but low quality

Use case: Diagnose specific failures when FID insufficient.

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
8.6 Training Challenges

8.6.1 Mode Collapse
Problem: Generator produces limited variety, ignoring parts of data distribution.
Symptoms:

Generated samples look similar
Low Recall metric
Discriminator loss oscillates

Fixes:

WGAN-GP (stable gradients)
Minibatch discrimination (penalize lack of diversity)
Unrolled GANs (look ahead in discriminator updates)




8.6.2 Vanishing Gradients
Problem: Discriminator becomes too strong → generator receives tiny or zero gradients.
Why it happens:
In the vanilla GAN objective, when \(D(G(z)) \to 0, \,\, \nabla_G \log (1 - D(G(z))) \to 0\).
Fixes:

Non-saturating loss: \(\max_G \mathbb{E}[\log D(G(z))]\)
Feature matching: Match statistics of discriminator’s intermediate features
One-sided label smoothing: Real labels = 0.9 (not 1.0)




8.6.3 Training Instability
Problem: GANs optimize a min–max game, not a single objective → unstable fixed point behavior. Training dynamics can oscillate wildly and the minmax game may fail to converge.
Symptoms:

Losses do not correlate with image quality
Discriminator and generator take turns “winning”
Sudden collapse in sample quality

Solutions:

Architecture Stabilization:

Spectral normalization → enforces Lipschitz constraint on \(D\)
Batch normalization in G (avoid in final layer of \(D\))
LeakyReLU in D → prevents dead units
Residual connections / skip connections (modern GANs)

Optimization stabilization

TTUR (Two-Time-Scale Update Rule):

# Two Time-Scale Update Rule (TTUR)
lr_D = 4e-4  # Higher discriminator learning rate
lr_G = 1e-4  # Lower generator learning rate
optimizer = Adam(lr, betas=(0.0, 0.9))  # Different from default

Balanced update ratio e.g., 1 D step, per 1 G step; or 5:1 in WGANs.

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
8.7 Training Monitoring
What to plot:
1. Losses (but interpret carefully):
# Discriminator loss should be stable, not too low
plot(D_loss_real, D_loss_fake, D_loss_total)

# Generator loss should decrease (but may oscillate)
plot(G_loss)
⚠️ Warning: GAN losses are NOT good indicators of quality!

Discriminator loss approaching 0 → too strong (generator gets no gradient)
Generator loss approaching 0 → fooling discriminator (might be mode collapse)
Oscillating losses can indicate healthy adversarial dynamics

2. Generated samples (most important):
# Save samples every N iterations
if iter % save_freq == 0:
    with torch.no_grad():
        fake = G(fixed_noise)  # Use same noise for comparison
        save_image(fake, f'samples_{iter}.png')
3. Evaluation metrics:
# Compute every epoch or few epochs
if epoch % eval_freq == 0:
    FID_score = compute_FID(real_images, generated_images)
    IS_score = compute_IS(generated_images)
    log(FID_score, IS_score)
Red flags:

Generator produces identical samples → mode collapse
Generator produces noise or blurry blobs → vanishing gradient
Discriminator loss drops to 0 early → generator stops improving (Discriminator is too strong)
Sudden quality degradation → training instability

title: 8  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
8.9 Interview Preparation

8.9.1 Core Concepts Checklist

GAN minimax objective and Nash equilibrium
Non-saturating loss vs saturating loss
Mode collapse: causes and solutions
Wasserstein distance vs JS divergence
WGAN-GP gradient penalty mechanism
FID vs Inception Score
StyleGAN architecture innovations




8.9.2 Key Interview Questions
Q1: “What is mode collapse and how do you prevent it?”
Answer: Mode collapse is when generator produces limited variety, ignoring parts of data distribution. Generator finds samples that fool discriminator and exploits these without exploring other modes.
Detection: Visual inspection (similar samples), low Recall metric, oscillating discriminator loss.
Solutions:

WGAN-GP (better gradients, less prone to collapse)
Minibatch discrimination (penalizes lack of diversity)
Multiple discriminators/generators


Q2: “Why use Wasserstein distance instead of Jensen-Shannon divergence?”
Answer: When real and fake sample distributions don’t overlap:

JS divergence stops providing learning signal,
since \(\text{JS}(p_{\text{data}} | p_g)  \equiv \log 2\) is constant when \(p_{\text{data}}\) and \(p_g\) have disjoint supports.
The Wasserstein distance gives non-zero gradients during training,
since it always measures the “cost” of moving probability mass from \(p_g\) to \(p_r\).

Advantages:

Continuous and differentiable everywhere
Provides meaningful gradients even with disjoint distributions
More stable training

Disadvantage:: Requires enforcing Lipschitz constraint (gradient penalty).

Q3: “Explain WGAN-GP’s gradient penalty. Why better than weight clipping?”
Answer:
Goal: Enforce 1-Lipschitz constraint on discriminator.
Weight clipping (original WGAN):

Limits capacity (parameters stuck at boundaries)
Pathological optimization surfaces

Why better: Soft constraint, discriminator uses full parameter space, smoother optimization.

Q5: “How do you evaluate GAN performance?”
Answer:
FID (primary metric):

Measures distance between real/generated distributions in feature space
Lower is better
Sensitive to mode collapse
Correlates with human judgment

Inception Score (secondary):

Measures sharpness and diversity
Doesn’t compare to real distribution
Can be fooled

Precision/Recall:

Separately measure quality vs diversity
Diagnose specific failures

Best practice: FID + visual inspection + Precision/Recall for diagnosis.
